- Caveats: CPSC recordings run 6–60 s, so you'll need to crop or pad them; INCART is 30-minute Holter-style data, so leave it out. Label quality also varies by source.

**3. Chapman-Shaoxing / Ningbo (PhysioNet: "A large scale 12-lead electrocardiogram database for arrhythmia study")**
- About 45,000 recordings, 10 s, 500 Hz, labeled by licensed physicians with SNOMED codes, including AV blocks and bundle branch blocks. It's heavy on rhythm labels, which suits AF.
- License is CC BY 4.0. Note that it overlaps with the Challenge collection above.

**4. CODE-15% (Zenodo), for large-scale pretraining**
- About 345,000 exams from 233,000 Brazilian patients, CC BY 4.0, no application needed.
- It has 6 labels, including AF, 1st-degree AV block, RBBB and LBBB.
- The labels come from automated analysis combined with text reports, not careful cardiologist review, so they're noisier. Recording length also varies (7–10 s).
- The separate CODE-test set (827 exams annotated by several cardiologists) makes a good external test set for these labels.

**Possible addition: MIMIC-IV-ECG.** It has about 800,000 10-s 12-lead ECGs and, as far as I know, the waveforms and machine-generated reports are open access. The labels are machine reports, though, and linking them to clinical data requires credentialing. Treat it as optional.

## Things to plan for

- **2nd- and 3rd-degree AV block are rare everywhere.** PTB-XL has only about a dozen examples of each. If high-grade AV block matters to you, pool data across sources, consider grouping the AV block classes, and report how much your confidence intervals widen with so few cases.
- **Split by patient, not by recording.** PTB-XL and CODE have repeat recordings from the same patients.
- **"Open access" still has terms.** CC BY means you must credit the dataset and cite its paper. More importantly, many institutions still want a short determination that secondary use of public, de-identified data is "not human subjects research." That's usually a quick form, not a full ethics review, but check with your IRB or ethics office before you publish.

**Suggested setup:** start with PTB-XL for development and benchmarking. Add the Challenge 2021 sources for training volume and testing on unseen hospitals, and use CODE-test as an external check for AF, bundle branch blocks and 1st-degree AV block.

cases.name: ho-h-measured-bp-surveys
cases.promptMarkdown: I'm writing an epidemiology thesis chapter on hypertension awareness, i.e. what share of adults with high blood pressure don't know they have it. For that I need nationally representative survey data where blood pressure was actually measured by a nurse or examiner, alongside a question on whether a doctor ever told them they have high blood pressure. Self-reported hypertension on its own is useless to me. Which surveys should I use, and what do I have to do to get each one?

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
I'd use **NHANES** as the core US source, with **ELSA (England)** and **CHARLS (China)** or **LASI (India)** for the international comparison. If you want the comparison to line up closely, add **HRS** as the US arm for ages 50+. All of these are free and you can have them within minutes to a few days.

**Where these facts come from:** I checked on 2026-11-12. Facts marked "today" came from the survey's own page or documentation. The rest is from memory, and you should check it in the codebooks before relying on it.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a national sample (an older-adult sample is fine), blood pressure measured by an examiner, a self-reported "ever told you have high blood pressure" question, antihypertensive medication (so treated people with normal readings still count as hypertensive), and survey weights.
- **Nice to have:** you can get the data within a few weeks with no fee.

## Shortlist
| # | Survey | Who's in it | Access | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US) | all ages | direct download, minutes | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US) | 50+ | free account, minutes | today (via HRS documentation) |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England) | 50+ | free UK Data Service account, 1–2 days | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China) | 45+ | registration plus approval, about 3 days | today (via web search) |
| 5 | **LASI** (India) | 45+ | registration through the Gateway to Global Aging Data | today (via web search) |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (South Korea) | all ages | free registration; the site is mostly in Korean | partly |
| 7 | **WHO SAGE** (6 low- and middle-income countries) | 50+ | registration plus a short request | from memory |
| 8 | **WHO STEPS** (many countries) | 18–69 | account plus a request for each country | partly |

## Details and how to get each one

**1. NHANES**: https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/
- **Variables (seen today):** BP is measured at the mobile exam centre, in file BPXO_L (`BPXOSY1`, `BPXODI1`, …). The awareness question is in BPQ_L: `BPQ020` asks "Have you ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension, also called high blood pressure?" The documentation says you must use the design variables and weights.
- **Steps:** pick a cycle, download the DEMO, BPXO (or BPX) and BPQ `.xpt` files, then merge them on `SEQN`.
- **Licence:** US public domain; cite NCHS.
- **Caveat:** the 2021–23 cycle measured BP with an automatic (oscillometric) device. Earlier cycles used the auscultatory (BPX) method, which matters if you look at trends.
- **Papers using it:** [Gu et al. 2008, AJH](https://doi.org/10.1038/ajh.2008.185) and [Gu et al. 2012, Circulation](https://doi.org/10.1161/circulationaha.112.096156).

**2. HRS**: https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/
- **Content:** since 2006, a random half of the sample gets an enhanced interview with physical measures each wave, including BP. The core interview asks about doctor-diagnosed high BP and medication (from memory).
- **Steps:** register for free, accept the Conditions of Use, and download the core files (Section I) or the RAND HRS longitudinal file.
- **Conditions:** you agree not to try to identify participants and not to pass the data to third parties.
- **Caveats:**
  - Trained interviewers measure BP, not nurses. That's still an objective measurement, but say so in your methods.
  - Each person is measured only every 4 years.
- **Why use it:** it is harmonised with ELSA, CHARLS and LASI through the Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org), which makes it the cleanest basis for a cross-national comparison.

**3. ELSA**: https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data
- **Access (seen today):** the ELSA site says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS"; non-UK users "can request a username."
- **Content (from memory):** nurse visits measure BP in waves 2, 4, 6 and 8/9, with diagnosis and medication questions and nurse-visit weights.
- **Steps:** register with the UK Data Service, accept the End User Licence, and download study SN 5050.

**4. CHARLS**: https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/
- **Content:** interviewers take three BP readings.
- **Steps:** register, sign the data-use agreement, and you get a password by email after about 3 days.
- **Caveat:** measured BP is confirmed for waves 1–3 (2011, 2013, 2015). Check whether 2018 and later waves have it.

**5. LASI**: https://lasi-india.org/data-instructions
- **Content:** wave 1 (2017–18), about 73,000 people.
- **Steps:** access is through the Gateway to Global Aging Data; registration is free with agreement to the data-use conditions.
- **Paper doing exactly your analysis:** [PLOS Med 2021](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1003740).

**6. KNHANES**: https://knhanes.kdca.go.kr
- **Why consider it:** it is the closest equivalent to NHANES outside the US: all ages, examiner-measured BP, free SAS/SPSS files.
- **Not confirmed:** whether foreign users can register without hurdles. The site and codebooks are largely in Korean.

**7 and 8. WHO SAGE and STEPS**
- **SAGE:** the paper on awareness in 6 countries ([IJE 2014](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyt215)) used it, but its data are from 2007–10.
- **STEPS:** many countries, but only ages 18–69, and access depends on the country.

## Known, not confirmed
I couldn't check these today, but as far as I know they have measured BP plus self-report:
- **Health Survey for England:** the HSE site blocked automated access; data are on the UK Data Service.
- **MHAS** (Mexico), **TILDA** (Ireland) and **ELSI-Brazil:** their sites didn't respond.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no BP measurement.
- **UK Biobank:** volunteers rather than a national sample, and the application is paid.
- **Canadian Health Measures Survey:** fits on content, but you can only use it inside a Statistics Canada Research Data Centre, which takes months.
- **CLSA:** application with a fee, and the sample isn't strictly representative.

## Next step
Which comparator to pick depends on the framing:
- **All adults:** compare NHANES with KNHANES or HSE.
- **Older adults:** compare HRS (plus NHANES restricted to ages 50+) with ELSA and CHARLS or LASI, using the Gateway harmonised files.

[This 2026 BMC Public Health paper](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-26341-4) looks at gaps in hypertension care across five national ageing cohorts. I haven't checked which cohorts it uses, but it would be worth reading as a template for the older-adult version.

Sources: [CHARLS user guide](https://charls.charlsdata.com/Public/ashelf/public/uploads/document/2011-charls-wave1/application/CHARLS_nationalbaseline_users_guide.pdf), [Gateway: CHARLS](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/05a8df66-b9ab-47de-879e-b0bde672798d), [Gateway: LASI](https://g2aging.org/additional-resources/gateway-blog/a1336913-5fb6-4198-b592-3802ef4729e8), [Gateway harmonised data](https://g2aging.org/harmonized-data/get-data), [HRS 2018 data description](https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/documentation/data-descriptions/1652380440/h18dd.pdf), [HRS public data overview](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/biblio/OverviewofHRSPublicData.pdf), [KNHANES profile (IJE)](https://academic.oup.com/ije/article/43/1/69/733063), [JKMS 2025](https://jkms.org/pdf/10.3346/jkms.2025.40.e189)

There's an interactive page where you can compare and filter the surveys and export an access plan: `/private/tmp/e-efRboB/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
I'd use **NHANES** as the US source. For the other countries, **ELSA (England)** and either **CHARLS (China)** or **LASI (India)** are the strongest options. All four put measured blood pressure and a "doctor ever told you" question on the same people. HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI are also sister studies, and ready-made cross-country versions of their variables are on the Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org). That makes the international comparison much easier.

I checked these on 12 Nov 2026. "Today" in the Checked column means I confirmed it from the official page or the study's own documents. "From memory" means I didn't. Access rules change, so re-check before you submit an ethics application.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** a nationally representative sample. Adults of all ages, or 45+/50+, is fine.
- **R2 (must):** blood pressure measured by a nurse, examiner or trained field staff.
- **R3 (must):** a "has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure" question, asked of the same people.
- **R4 (nice to have):** you can get the data within weeks on a student's standing.

## Shortlist
| # | Survey | Access | Who measured BP | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES** (US, all ages) | Direct download, no account | Health technicians at mobile exam centres | today |
| 2 | **HRS** (US, 50+) | Free registration | Trained interviewers, not nurses | today, from HRS documents |
| 3 | **ELSA** (England, 50+) | Free UK Data Service account and End User Licence, ~days | Nurses (waves 2, 4, 6, 8, 9) | today |
| 4 | **CHARLS** (China, 45+) | Registration plus online agreement, approved in ~3 working days | Trained staff, 3 Omron readings | today, from the CHARLS FAQ |
| 5 | **LASI** (India, 45+, ~72,000 people) | Request form plus short proposal (~weeks), or through g2aging.org | Trained staff | today |
| 6 | **KNHANES** (Korea, all ages) | Registration and data request | Examiners | partly |
| 7 | **TILDA** (Ireland, 50+) | Public file through ISSDA (Irish Social Science Data Archive); fuller data by application, possibly with fees | Nurses | today |
| 8 | **Canadian Health Measures Survey** (CHMS) | Only inside Statistics Canada Research Data Centres, ~months | Mobile clinic staff | access rules from memory |

## Details
**1. NHANES** ([wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/))
- **Variables:** BP readings are in the BPX/BPXO files (automated cuff from 2017 onward). The awareness question is BPQ020. I confirmed its wording today: "ever been told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension, also called high blood pressure?" Related items are BPQ030 (told on 2+ visits) and BPQ150 (taking prescribed BP medication).
- **Steps:**
  - Download the DEMO, BPXO and BPQ files for a cycle and merge them on SEQN.
  - Use the exam weights plus the design variables SDMVSTRA and SDMVPSU.
- **Watch out for:**
  - The 2021–2023 cycle used a new sample design, so read the analysis guidelines before pooling it with earlier cycles.
  - The switch from manual to automated BP measurement affects trend analyses.
- **Example paper:** Egan et al., JAMA 2010 ([doi](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.650)), uses the standard awareness definition.

**2. HRS** ([New User Guide](https://hrs.isr.umich.edu/sites/default/files/new-user-guide/HRS-New-User-Guide-July-2025.pdf), [physical-measures documentation DR-011](https://hrsonline.isr.umich.edu/sitedocs/userg/dr-011.pdf))
- **Variables:** BP was measured with an Omron HEM-780 during the in-person interview from 2006 onward. Each half of the sample is measured every 4 years.
- **Access:** BP is in the public core files and needs only registration. The blood biomarkers need an extra sensitive-data agreement.
- **Weights:** use the physical-measures weights (KPMWGTR for 2006, NPMWGTR for 2012).
- **Watch out for:** interviewers took the readings, not nurses. If your examiners must be nurses, say this in your methods.

**3. ELSA** ([how to access the data](https://www.elsa-project.ac.uk/accessing-elsa-data), [nurse visit user guide](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/population-health-sciences/sites/population_health_sciences/files/5050_elsa_waves_2-4-6-8-9_nurse_data_user_guide.pdf))
- **Access:** the ELSA site says: "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS."
- **Steps:**
  - Register with the UK Data Service. Use your institution's login (UKAMF) if your institution is a member, otherwise request a username.
  - Download study SN 5050, which includes the nurse files, and use the nurse weights.

**4. CHARLS** ([FAQ](https://charls.pku.edu.cn/en/Faq/Frequently_Asked_Questions.htm))
- **Variables:** the question is "Have you ever been diagnosed with hypertension by a doctor?" BP is measured as three Omron HEM-7200 readings.
- **Steps:**
  - Register at charls.pku.edu.cn and sign the online data-use agreement.
  - Activate your account by email, then apply for each dataset. The FAQ says approval takes about 3 working days.
  - Use the official site only, not the unofficial copies that circulate online.
- **Example papers:** [BMJ Open 2016](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-009836) compares self-reported and measured hypertension. [BMC Public Health](https://bmcpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12889-019-6753-x) looks at awareness from 2011 to 2015.

**5. LASI** ([request form](https://iipsindia.ac.in/sites/default/files/LASI_DataRequestForm_0.pdf), [cohort profile](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyab266))
- **Variables:** the question is "Has any health professional ever told you that you have hypertension or high blood pressure?"
- **Steps:** email the form, a 500-word description of your topic and a study proposal to datacenter@iipsindia.ac.in. Alternatively, register on g2aging.org for the harmonised version.
- **Example paper:** [PMC8425529](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8425529) covers awareness, treatment and control in India.

**6–8.**
- **KNHANES:** the closest copy of NHANES's design. Literature found in a web search today says the raw data need registration and a request. KNHANES's English page returned a 404 today, and the site is mostly in Korean. I couldn't tell whether researchers outside Korea can register.
- **TILDA:** the site says the data are "only available for access by non-commercial entities." The fuller health data go through the VISTA remote secure environment or on-site desks, and fees may apply. I haven't checked which BP variables are in the public ISSDA file.
- **CHMS:** realistic only if you have a Canadian affiliation.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Health Survey for England:** nurse-measured BP, distributed through the UK Data Service. Its site blocked my automated check. ELSA already includes an HSE baseline ("wave 0").
- **Indonesia Family Life Survey (IFLS):** measured BP, free registration through RAND, from memory. RAND's site blocked the check.
- **WHO SAGE** (six low- and middle-income countries, measured BP): the catalogue page resolves, but I didn't read its access terms.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** measured BP in a subsample only (from memory). I didn't confirm it.

## Not recommended, and why
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only.
- **SHARE:** no measured BP in its core waves (from memory).
- **UK Biobank:** a volunteer cohort, not nationally representative, and fee-based.

## What I could not find
The general dataset registries returned nothing relevant. Every candidate came from my own knowledge, the literature and web searches, which is normal for national surveys.

## Next step
Start downloading NHANES today. At the same time, register with the UK Data Service for ELSA and with CHARLS, which should take a few days. If you'd like India instead of, or as well as, China, send the LASI request now, because it takes the longest. Before you analyse anything, fix one definition of "unaware" across all surveys: measured BP ≥140/90 (or ≥130/80), or on BP medication, but not reporting a diagnosis. Also note how many readings each survey averages, because that differs between them.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-jq5eMJ/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

| 1 | **NHANES** (US, all ages) | Certified examiners in a mobile exam centre | Free download, no login | minutes | today |

**3. ELSA.** The ELSA site says "End User Licence level data are available to all via UKDS" (confirmed today). Log in through your institution (UK Access Management Federation) or request a username if you're outside the UK. Then download the ELSA series, including the nurse files.
- **Nurse visits:** only every other wave (2, 4, 6, 8/9, from memory). COVID affected later waves.
- **Wave 0:** this is the Health Survey for England, which also has nurse-measured BP for all ages.

**4. CHARLS.** The documentation says the data are "freely available to all bona fide researchers." You register at charls.pku.edu.cn/en and submit a request. The site timed out from here, so check the current form yourself.
- **Waves:** use 2011–2018. The 2020 wave apparently had no physical exam, but I couldn't confirm that.
- **Use:** there is a CHARLS paper on hypertension awareness ([PMC6480849](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6480849/)).

**5. LASI.** Fill in the request form at https://www.iipsindia.ac.in/content/lasi-data and attach "a valid identity proof." Access is "only granted for legitimate academic research purposes", and IIPS reviews requests "within 24 to 48 hours" (all confirmed today). With about 73,000 respondents it gives a high-undiagnosed contrast to the US and England.

**6. KNHANES.** Register on knhanes.kdca.go.kr, accept the data use policy and download the raw files. The registration pages are mostly in Korean, and I couldn't confirm that foreign researchers can sign up.

## Not recommended
- **NHIS and BRFSS:** self-reported hypertension only, so they fail your main requirement.
- **SHARE:** as far as I recall, no BP measurement in the main survey.
- **MHAS (Mexico):** BP was measured only in a subsample, from memory, and I couldn't confirm the site.
- **TILDA and CHMS:** they fit the measurement requirement, but access is slower. TILDA needs an application and is for non-commercial users only. CHMS can only be used inside a Canadian Research Data Centre.

- **Who did the measuring differs:** examiners (NHANES), nurses (ELSA) and trained interviewers or field staff (HRS, CHARLS, LASI). Say this in your methods.
- **A single visit overestimates hypertension:** every survey here measures BP on one occasion, not over repeated visits. graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
For the US, use **NHANES**. For the comparison countries, I'd use **ELSA** (England) and either **CHARLS** (China) or **KNHANES** (South Korea). All four measure blood pressure as part of an exam and also ask whether a doctor ever told the respondent they have high blood pressure, so you can count people who meet the measured or medication definition but say they were never told.

## 1. NHANES (United States): your main survey

- **Why:** It's a nationally representative sample of all ages. Blood pressure is measured at a mobile exam centre (MEC), and CDC uses it for its own official figures on hypertension awareness. CDC Data Brief 511 reports these for Aug 2021–Aug 2023 (prevalence 47.7%), so you can check your numbers against it.
- **Files for the latest cycle (2021–2023, suffix `_L`):**
  - `BPXO_L`: three oscillometric readings (`BPXOSY1–3`, `BPXODI1–3`).
  - `BPQ_L`: the questionnaire with "ever told you had high blood pressure" and BP medication use.
  - `DEMO_L`: demographics, plus the survey design variables (`SDMVSTRA`, `SDMVPSU`) and the exam weight (`WTMEC2YR`).
- **Access:** None needed. The public XPT files download freely from the CDC NHANES site, with no registration.
- **Things to watch:**
  - From 2021 NHANES switched from auscultatory readings (`BPX` files in older cycles) to oscillometric ones. If you pool or trend across cycles, the protocol change matters.
  - Use the MEC exam weights, not the interview weights, and account for the survey design (stratum and PSU).
  - The 2017–March 2020 "pre-pandemic" file is the previous usable cycle.

## 2. ELSA (England, ages 50+): best match for older adults

- **Why:** It's a nationally representative sample of people aged 50 and over. A study nurse measures blood pressure at a home visit, following the Health Survey for England protocol. The core interview asks about doctor-diagnosed high blood pressure, and the nurse visit also records prescribed medications.
- **Which waves:** Nurse visits took place in waves 2, 4, 6, 8 and 9. In wave 9 (2018/19) only half the sample got a visit. Use the nurse-visit weights.
- **Access:**
  1. Register with the UK Data Service (study SN 5050).
  2. Accept the End User Licence, which is free for academic use.
  3. Download.

  I think the main nurse files are in the End User Licence release, but I couldn't confirm that. Check the access level on the SN 5050 catalogue page. Some variables are under Special Licence, which takes a short extra application.
- **Contact:** ELSAdata@natcen.ac.uk.

## 3. A third survey: choose one

- **CHARLS (China, ages 45+):** It's nationally representative. Trained field staff take three Omron readings rather than nurses, and you get the doctor-diagnosis question and medication use. It's widely used for studies of hypertension awareness. **Access:** register free on the CHARLS website (charls.pku.edu.cn), state how you'll use the data, and download once approved, usually within days.
- **KNHANES (South Korea, all ages):** It's built on the NHANES model, so it's the closest match in design: standardized measurement by trained examiners, plus a diagnosis question. **Access:** register free on the KDCA KNHANES site and submit a short data request. The documentation is partly in English.
- **Also possible:** LASI (India, 45+) has the same type of design as CHARLS. You request it through IIPS or the Gateway to Global Aging. HRS, the US sister study to ELSA, has had physical measures including BP, taken by interviewers in half the sample each wave since 2006, but NHANES is the stronger US source.

**Practical tip:** ELSA, CHARLS, LASI and HRS are harmonized by the **Gateway to Global Aging Data** (g2aging.org). It publishes consistent variable definitions across studies, which makes cross-country comparisons much easier to defend in a thesis.

**Methods points to settle early:**
- Pick one threshold, 140/90 or ACC/AHA 130/80, and apply it everywhere. Report the other one as a sensitivity analysis.
- Define "hypertensive" as measured high BP *or* taking BP medication.
- Average the readings the same way in every survey (e.g., the mean of the 2nd and 3rd).
- Note the measurement differences: nurse versus trained interviewer, and oscillometric versus auscultatory.

Sources:
- [NHANES 2021–2023 Examination Data](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/search/datapage.aspx?Component=Examination&Cycle=2021-2023)
- [NHANES 2021–2023 Questionnaire Data](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/search/datapage.aspx?Component=Questionnaire&Cycle=2021-2023)
- [NCHS Data Brief 511](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db511.htm)
- [ELSA Wave 4 Nurse Dataset User Guide](https://ifs.org.uk/sites/default/files/output_url_files/wave_4_nurse_dataset.pdf)
- [ELSA Wave 9 Technical Report (UKDS SN 5050)](https://doc.ukdataservice.ac.uk/doc/5050/mrdoc/pdf/5050_elsa_w9_technical_report_v3.pdf)
- [UKDS ELSA update](https://ukdataservice.ac.uk/app/uploads/pacchiotti.pdf)
- [ELSA on Atlas of Longitudinal Datasets](https://atlaslongitudinaldatasets.ac.uk/datasets/elsa)

graders.name: 01-recall-nhanes
graders.evidence:
For your question the core requirement is a measured-BP-plus-diagnosis survey. NHANES is the obvious US choice. For international comparison, the HRS "sister studies" (ELSA, CHARLS, LASI) and Korea's KNHANES work best. I wrote this from memory and didn't check the websites this session, so confirm wave years and access steps against current documentation before citing them.

## United States

### 1. NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey): use this as your primary source
- **Why it fits:** It is the standard source for US hypertension awareness estimates. It is nationally representative of the civilian non-institutionalized population. Trained examiners measure BP in a mobile examination center (MEC), using up to three readings. Older cycles used a manual cuff. Since 2017–2018 an automated oscillometric protocol is used (files `BPXO_*`; earlier files are `BPX_*`).
- **Key variables:**
  - `BPQ020`: "Ever told by a doctor or other health professional that you had hypertension/high blood pressure?"
  - `BPQ040A`/`BPQ050A`: told to take, and now taking, BP medication. You need these to define hypertension as measured high BP *or* on medication.
- **Access:** Free public-use files (SAS XPT format), no registration. Download from the CDC/NCHS NHANES site (wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes). In R, the `nhanesA` package fetches files directly.
- **What you must do:**
  - Merge the demographics (DEMO), BP exam (BPX/BPXO) and BP questionnaire (BPQ) files on `SEQN`.
  - Use the **MEC exam weights** (`WTMEC2YR`, or the special weights for the 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic file) with `SDMVPSU`/`SDMVSTRA` in a survey-design analysis (R `survey`, Stata `svy`).
  - Follow the NCHS analytic guidelines when combining cycles.
- **Watch out for:**
  - The switch from manual to oscillometric measurement. NCHS ran a crossover comparison in 2017–2018, which you should cite if you look at trends.
  - COVID disrupted collection. There is a 2017–March 2020 pre-pandemic file and then a separate August 2021–August 2023 cycle.

### 2. HRS (Health and Retirement Study), ages 50+: optional
- Interviewers measure BP during in-home "enhanced face-to-face" interviews, with each random half of the sample measured every other wave since 2006. HRS also asks whether a doctor ever told the respondent they have high BP.
- Access is free after registering on the HRS website (University of Michigan). The physical measures are in the public core files. Blood biomarkers carry extra restrictions, but you don't need them.
- Use it only if you need longitudinal data or exact comparability with the international aging studies below. Note that interviewers take the readings, not nurses, so mention that if you're strict about who measures.

## International comparisons

**Option A: Harmonized aging studies (best for comparability with HRS, or with NHANES restricted to ages 50+)**
- **ELSA (English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, 50+):** A nurse visit with BP measurement took place roughly every other wave (2, 4, 6 and 8/9), and the survey has a doctor-diagnosis question. Access is through the **UK Data Service**: register, accept the End User Licence, and it's free for academic use. The nurse-visit data sit in separate files and have their own weights.
- **CHARLS (China, 45+):** Trained staff measure BP with Omron devices (2011, 2013 and 2015 are the main waves with physical measures; check later waves). It asks about doctor-diagnosed hypertension. Free after registering on the CHARLS site at Peking University.
- **LASI (India, 45+, Wave 1 2017–19):** Measured BP plus a diagnosis question, with a very large sample. You apply through IIPS / the LASI data portal.
- **Tip:** The **Gateway to Global Aging Data** (g2aging.org) offers harmonized versions of HRS, ELSA, CHARLS and LASI with consistent variable definitions. That saves a lot of recoding and gives you a citable harmonization source.

**Option B: An NHANES clone**
- **KNHANES (Korea):** Modeled directly on NHANES. Trained examiners measure BP, there is a doctor-diagnosis question, it covers all ages, and it runs annually. Download it free after registering on the KDCA KNHANES website. Some documentation is Korean-only.
- **CHMS (Canadian Health Measures Survey)** is also comparable, but microdata access requires a Statistics Canada Research Data Centre application, which is slow for a thesis.

**Avoid:** SHARE (Europe) for this question. Except for limited sub-studies, it doesn't measure BP, so you'd be back to self-report.

## My recommendation
Use **NHANES** as the core. Add **ELSA** plus either **CHARLS** or **LASI** through the Gateway harmonized files. If you want a high-income, all-ages comparator with the same design, use **KNHANES** instead. Restrict every sample to the same age band (e.g., 50+) for the comparison.

## Methods points examiners will ask about
1. **Definition:**
   - Hypertension = mean SBP ≥140 or DBP ≥90 (or ≥130/80 under the 2017 ACC/AHA definition), **or** current antihypertensive use.
   - Unaware = has hypertension but answered "no" to the doctor-told question.
   - Report results under both thresholds.
2. **Readings:** Most studies average the 2nd and 3rd readings and drop the first. Apply the same rule across all surveys.
3. **Single-visit bias:** Clinical diagnosis needs repeated visits, but these surveys measure once. That overstates prevalence and therefore "unawareness." Acknowledge it as a limitation.
4. **Device and protocol differences** across surveys (manual vs. oscillometric, examiner type) limit direct comparisons. Describe them in a table.

2. **Readings:** Most studies average the 2nd and 3rd readings and drop the first. Apply the same rule across all surveys.
3. **Single-visit bias:** Clinical diagnosis needs repeated visits, but these surveys measure once. That overstates prevalence and therefore "unawareness." Acknowledge it as a limitation.
4. **Device and protocol differences** across surveys (manual vs. oscillometric, examiner type) limit direct comparisons. Describe them in a table.

- **Measurement:** Blood pressure is measured by a **nurse** during nurse-visit waves: 2, 4, 6, and the 8/9 period. Check the exact years in the documentation.

For this, NHANES should be your main dataset. Add HRS if you want an older-US sample. For other countries, the best matches are the HRS "sister studies": ELSA (England), CHARLS (China) and LASI (India). All of them measure blood pressure and ask whether a doctor ever told the person they have high blood pressure, and harmonized versions exist. I wrote this from what I already know and didn't check the websites live, so confirm current releases and access rules before you cite them.

## United States

### 1. NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey): main dataset
- **Why:** It's the standard source for US hypertension awareness. It covers the civilian non-institutionalized population of all ages. Blood pressure is measured by trained examiners in Mobile Examination Centers.
- **Key variables:**
  - `BPQ020` asks: "Ever told by a doctor or other health professional that you had high blood pressure?"
  - `BPQ050A` asks whether the person is currently taking blood pressure medication. You need this to separate "treated" from "aware."
  - The exam files are `BPX` (older cycles) and `BPXO` (oscillometric, 2017 onward).
- **Watch out:** The method changed. Older cycles used auscultation with a mercury device. 2017–March 2020 had both methods, and later cycles (e.g., August 2021–August 2023) are oscillometric only. If you pool across this change or look at trends, say so and consider calibration. Use the exam weights (`WTMEC2YR`, or the pre-pandemic combined weights) and the design variables `SDMVSTRA`/`SDMVPSU`.
- **Access:** Free download from the CDC/NCHS NHANES website in SAS XPT format, with no registration. Restricted variables, such as detailed geography, require an application to the NCHS Research Data Center. The R package `nhanesA` or Python `pandas.read_sas` will load the files.

### 2. HRS (Health and Retirement Study): adults aged 50+
- **Why:** Useful as an older-adult US estimate and as the anchor for comparing with other countries.
- **Measurement:** Since 2006, a random half of the sample gets physical measures in a face-to-face interview each wave, so each person is measured every 4 years. Three readings are taken with an Omron monitor by **trained interviewers, not nurses**. Say this in your methods section.
- **Question:** "Has a doctor ever told you that you have high blood pressure or hypertension?"
- **Access:** Free registration at hrsonline.isr.umich.edu. The biomarker and physical-measure files are public. The RAND HRS longitudinal file makes the data much easier to work with. Sensitive or restricted files need a separate application.

## Other countries (middle-aged and older adults)

### 3. ELSA (English Longitudinal Study of Ageing): adults aged 50+, England
- **Measurement:** Blood pressure is measured by a **nurse** during nurse-visit waves: 2, 4, 6, and the 8/9 period. Check the exact years in the documentation.
- **Access:** UK Data Service (study SN 5050). You register, accept the End User Licence, and download for free. The nurse-visit data are in separate files within the study.
- **Alternative:** The Health Survey for England covers all ages, with nurse-measured blood pressure and a doctor-diagnosis question, through the same UK Data Service process. Nurse visits were suspended around COVID, so check which recent years include them.

### 4. CHARLS (China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study): adults aged 45+
- **Measurement:** Trained interviewers take repeated readings with an Omron device. This was done in 2011, 2013 and 2015, and possibly 2018. The 2020 wave was mostly by phone and has no physical measures, so check the documentation for 2018 onward.
- **Access:** Free registration and a data request at charls.pku.edu.cn.

### 5. LASI (Longitudinal Ageing Study in India): adults aged 45+
- **Measurement:** Wave 1 (2017–19) measured blood pressure and asked about doctor diagnosis. The sample is very large and nationally representative. Awareness of hypertension is known to be low in India, which could give your chapter a striking contrast with the US.
- **Access:** Request through IIPS Mumbai, or through the Gateway to Global Aging Data (below).

### Shortcut: Gateway to Global Aging Data (g2aging.org)
This site provides harmonized files for HRS, ELSA, CHARLS, LASI, MHAS (Mexico) and others, with standardized blood pressure and diagnosis variables. One free registration gets you the harmonized files plus codebooks. You still need permission from each original study to get its raw data. This is the easiest way to make your cross-country comparison methodologically clean.

### Other options
- **KNHANES (Korea):** All ages, nationally representative, modeled on NHANES, with examiner-measured blood pressure. Free download after registering on the KDCA website. This is the closest one-to-one match to NHANES if you want a comparison that isn't limited to older adults.
- **CHMS (Canada):** Good measurement, but microdata are mostly available only through Statistics Canada Research Data Centres.
- **Avoid SHARE** (Europe) for this question. It generally doesn't measure blood pressure.

## Methods points to settle early
- **Hypertension definition:** Use 140/90 or 130/80 (ACC/AHA 2017). Count people on blood pressure medication as hypertensive, whatever their measured value.
- **Readings:** Average the 2nd and 3rd readings, or all valid readings, and keep it the same across surveys.
- **Awareness:** Measure it among people with hypertension, as doctor-diagnosed or on medication, divided by everyone with hypertension (measured or treated).
- **Who measured:** Nurses or examiners in NHANES and ELSA, lay interviewers in HRS, CHARLS and LASI. This can bias the comparison, so mention it as a limitation.

A practical setup would be NHANES as the main analysis, with HRS, ELSA and CHARLS or LASI via g2aging for the 50+ cross-country comparison. If you want help writing the NHANES code (weights, merging the `BPQ` and `BPXO` files, and the awareness estimate in R `survey` or Stata `svy`), I can do that.

cases.name: ho-h-wrist-activity-outcomes
cases.promptMarkdown: I want to study whether physical activity and sleep patterns measured in daily life by wrist-worn accelerometers or activity trackers predict later disease and death. I need data from at least a few thousand adults who wore the device on the wrist for several days to a week or longer, linked to follow-up outcomes such as hospital records, diagnoses or death registrations. Wrist placement matters to me because I want my results to be comparable with other wrist-based studies. I'm at a US university and happy to go through applications. Which datasets should I consider, and what does getting access involve for each?

graders.name: 01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometer
graders.graderMarkdown: PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the "UK Biobank accelerometer" data (also called the UK Biobank physical activity monitor or accelerometry sub-study; about 100,000 UK Biobank participants who wore an Axivity AX3 wrist accelerometer for seven days, linked to hospital, cancer and death records) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. Recommending UK Biobank in a way that refers to its wrist accelerometer data also counts. FAIL if the answer does not mention UK Biobank's accelerometer data, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

config.criteria: PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the "UK Biobank accelerometer" data (also called the UK Biobank physical activity monitor or accelerometry sub-study; about 100,000 UK Biobank participants who wore an Axivity AX3 wrist accelerometer for seven days, linked to hospital, cancer and death records) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. Recommending UK Biobank in a way that refers to its wrist accelerometer data also counts. FAIL if the answer does not mention UK Biobank's accelerometer data, or mentions it only to say it is unsuitable.

graders.name: 02-recall-nhanes-wrist
graders.graderMarkdown: PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the NHANES wrist accelerometer data from the 2011-2012 and/or 2013-2014 cycles (the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey "Physical Activity Monitor" data, ActiGraph worn on the non-dominant wrist for seven days, often used with the NCHS linked mortality files) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. Recommending "NHANES accelerometry" without naming the cycle also counts, unless the answer points only to the 2003-2006 cycles. FAIL if the answer does not mention NHANES accelerometer data, mentions only the 2003-2006 accelerometer cycles, or mentions NHANES accelerometry only to say it is unsuitable.

config.criteria: PASS if the final answer recommends or lists the NHANES wrist accelerometer data from the 2011-2012 and/or 2013-2014 cycles (the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey "Physical Activity Monitor" data, ActiGraph worn on the non-dominant wrist for seven days, often used with the NCHS linked mortality files) as a candidate dataset for the user's question. Recommending "NHANES accelerometry" without naming the cycle also counts, unless the answer points only to the 2003-2006 cycles. graders.graderMarkdown: PASS if the final answer does not present the NHANES 2003-2004 and 2005-2006 accelerometer data as wrist-worn data. graders.name: 01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometer
graders.evidence:
The best dataset for your question is UK Biobank, but it is not taking new applications right now. NHANES 2011–14 is the one you can download and start on today, though it only links to deaths. All of Us, Whitehall II and China Kadoorie Biobank are the other main options. All of these facts were checked on 12 Nov 2026.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** the device was worn on the wrist. I counted consumer trackers like Fitbit as well as research accelerometers.
- **R2 (must):** free-living wear for several days to a week or more.
- **R3 (must):** at least a few thousand adults with device data.
- **R4 (must):** linked follow-up such as hospital records, diagnoses or death registrations.
- **R5 (nice to have, my assumption):** raw or minute-level signal, so you can compute activity and sleep metrics the same way other wrist studies do.
- **R6 (must):** a researcher at a US university can get it. You said waiting for an application is fine.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device, wear | N | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES 2011–14 + public Linked Mortality File** | Open download, minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, non-dominant wrist, 7 days | ~12,600 (all ages) | Deaths to end of 2019 | today (Medicare linkage from memory) |
| 2 | **UK Biobank accelerometer study** | Fee and application; **new applications closed**, reopening targeted for "late 2026" | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days | ~100,000 | Hospital records, primary care, cancer, deaths | today (closure, fees); outcome detail from papers |
| 3 | **All of Us (Fitbit + health records)** | Your institution's agreement plus training, a few days | Fitbit, months to years | ~15,000 (2023); recent studies 29,000–44,000 | Health-record diagnoses; deaths partial | today (tiers); death completeness from memory |
| 4 | **Whitehall II accelerometer study** | Application via Dementias Platform UK, months | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days | ~4,200 valid | Hospital records (from memory) and deaths | today |
| 5 | **China Kadoorie Biobank resurvey 2020–21** | Application plus £2,500, months; may still be closed to outsiders | Axivity AX3, wrist, 7 days | ~20,000 | Hospitalisation and deaths (from memory); short follow-up | partly today |
| 6 | **MESA Sleep (wrist actigraphy)** | Data agreement, days; event data by separate request, weeks | Actiwatch, 7 days | ~2,200 | Confirmed heart events, deaths | today (actigraphy); event route from memory |
| 7 | **MrOS / SOF actigraphy** | Analysis proposal, weeks | SleepWatch-O, 3–5 days | ~3,100 men, ~3,000 women | Fractures, hospitalisations, deaths | from memory |

## Details

**1. NHANES 2011–2014 + Linked Mortality File (start here)**
- **Links:** [PAXMIN_G documentation](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2011/DataFiles/PAXMIN_G.htm), [linked mortality files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm).
- **Data:** about 12,600 participants have minute-level activity data plus day and hour summaries. Adults link to the National Death Index through 31 Dec 2019.
- **Steps:**
  1. Download PAXMIN, PAXDAY, PAXHR and the demographics files for both waves.
  2. Download the `NHANES_2013_2014_MORT_2019_PUBLIC.dat` file and its 2011–12 equivalent from CDC's FTP site.
  3. Merge on the participant ID, `SEQN`.
- **Ready-made step counts:** an [open (CC0) PhysioNet version with minute-level step counts](https://physionet.org/content/minute-level-step-count-nhanes/1.0.2/) is also available.

  2. Submit the project application.

- **Data:** wrist actigraphy downloads from the [National Sleep Research Resource](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mesa) under its data agreement. Confirmed events and deaths come separately via BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center (from memory).

- **Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging:** wrist ActiGraph, about 1,000+ people; probably too small. Access is by proposal ([how to apply](https://www.blsa.nih.gov/how-apply), which blocked my check).
- **Rotterdam Study:** wrist GENEActiv or actigraphy, about 2,000.
- **HCHS/SOL Sueño:** wrist Actiwatch, about 2,000; via the National Sleep Research Resource and BioLINCC.
- **Pelotas 1982 cohort:** about 3,000 adults with wrist GENEActiv, but little disease follow-up.

All of these are from memory; check their size and outcome linkage.

## Not recommended
- **NHANES 2003–06:** hip-worn device.
- **Women's Health Initiative OPACH and Women's Health Study:** hip-worn (from memory).
- **HUNT4, Tromsø, 1970 British Cohort Study:** thigh, back or hip placement (from memory).
- **CAPTURE-24:** wrist and open, but about 150 people with no health outcomes. It is only useful for validating activity classifiers.

- The registry searches turned up almost nothing relevant; the candidates came from the literature and the web.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check this week whether your university has an All of Us DURA, and apply.
3. Register on the UK Biobank and DPUK portals so you can submit once UK Biobank reopens. Whitehall II is useful as a second wrist cohort to replicate your UK Biobank results.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-IgJsbM/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **NHANES 2011–14 + public Linked Mortality File** | Open download, minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, non-dominant wrist, 7 days | ~12,600 (all ages) | Deaths to end of 2019 | today (Medicare linkage from memory) |
| 2 | **UK Biobank accelerometer study** | Fee and application; **new applications closed**, reopening targeted for "late 2026" | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days | ~100,000 | Hospital records, primary care, cancer, deaths | today (closure, fees); outcome detail from papers |
| 3 | **All of Us (Fitbit + health records)** | Your institution's agreement plus training, a few days | Fitbit, months to years | ~15,000 (2023); recent studies 29,000–44,000 | Health-record diagnoses; deaths partial | today (tiers); death completeness from memory |
| 4 | **Whitehall II accelerometer study** | Application via Dementias Platform UK, months | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days | ~4,200 valid | Hospital records (from memory) and deaths | today |

**1. NHANES 2011–2014 + Linked Mortality File (start here)**

  1. Download PAXMIN, PAXDAY, PAXHR and the demographics files for both waves.
  2. Download the `NHANES_2013_2014_MORT_2019_PUBLIC.dat` file and its 2011–12 equivalent from CDC's FTP site.
  3. Merge on the participant ID, `SEQN`.

- **Restricted data:** exact death dates or Medicare claims need an application to an NCHS Research Data Center (months, from memory).
- **Limits:** death is the only outcome, follow-up is about 6–8 years, and the public file slightly alters some variables.
- **Papers using it:** a 2024 study found [physical activity was the strongest predictor of death](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/); another used [activity profiles as markers of mortality](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-36062-y).

- **Why it matters:** this is the reference wrist cohort. Linked hospital records, primary care, cancer registry and death data support analyses across hundreds of diseases, for example [MVPA vs 697 diseases](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-022-00676-9) and [sleep regularity and mortality](https://doi.org/10.7554/elife.88359.3).
- **Current status (confirmed today):** after an April 2026 data incident, all access was suspended. [UK Biobank's own FAQ](https://community.ukbiobank.ac.uk/hc/en-gb/articles/37284734505117-Can-I-apply-to-use-UK-Biobank-data) says "We are not currently accepting applications for new research projects" and that they aim to reopen in late 2026. When existing projects return, exporting results will be temporarily banned.
- **Steps once it reopens:**
  1. Register yourself and your institution on the Access Management System.
  2. Submit the project application.
  3. Sign the Material Transfer Agreement through your institution.
  4. Pay the [fee](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/): Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years, or £500 for students.
  5. Analyse on the cloud platform (UKB-RAP), where compute is billed.

**3. All of Us**

- **Data:** 4,880 people were asked in 2012–13 to wear a GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, and 4,204 have valid data. Published work processes the raw files with the GGIR software.

- **To check:** whether outside users can get the linked hospital records through DPUK.
- **Limits:** mostly male, white-collar civil servants.
- **Paper using it:** [mortality in Whitehall II and UK Biobank (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-30237-5).

**5. China Kadoorie Biobank**
- **Data:** same device and protocol as UK Biobank ([descriptive paper](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)).
- **Access:** register on their data access system and apply online; approved requests from outside China cost £2,500 ([policy](https://www.ckbiobank.org/data-access/data-2)).
- **To check:** new data are reserved for the study's own researchers for a period first. I could not confirm whether the accelerometer data have been released yet. Look at their data overview and release schedule, or propose a collaboration.

**6. MESA Sleep**
- **Data:** wrist actigraphy downloads from the [National Sleep Research Resource](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mesa) under its data agreement. Confirmed events and deaths come separately via BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center (from memory).
- **Paper using it:** [sleep regularity and mortality](https://doi.org/10.1111/jsr.14048).
- **Limits:** N is below your target, and Actiwatch counts are not directly comparable with the metrics other wrist studies use.

**7. MrOS / SOF**
- **Data:** the National Sleep Research Resource's MrOS page says actigraphy is not included there. Use MrOS Online, or send an analysis proposal to the San Francisco Coordinating Center.
- **Limits:** older adults only, 3–5 days of wear.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging:** wrist ActiGraph, about 1,000+ people; probably too small. Access is by proposal ([how to apply](https://www.blsa.nih.gov/how-apply), which blocked my check).
- **Rotterdam Study:** wrist GENEActiv or actigraphy, about 2,000.
- **HCHS/SOL Sueño:** wrist Actiwatch, about 2,000; via the National Sleep Research Resource and BioLINCC.
- **Pelotas 1982 cohort:** about 3,000 adults with wrist GENEActiv, but little disease follow-up.

All of these are from memory; check their size and outcome linkage.

## Not recommended
- **NHANES 2003–06:** hip-worn device.
- **Women's Health Initiative OPACH and Women's Health Study:** hip-worn (from memory).
- **HUNT4, Tromsø, 1970 British Cohort Study:** thigh, back or hip placement (from memory).
- **CAPTURE-24:** wrist and open, but about 150 people with no health outcomes. It is only useful for validating activity classifiers.

## What I could not find
- No openly downloadable wrist dataset linked to hospital records; NHANES only links to deaths.
- Several official sites (UK Biobank, UCL, CKB, sleepdata.org) blocked automated checks, so I took those facts from web-search summaries of the pages or from memory, as marked.
- The registry searches turned up almost nothing relevant; the candidates came from the literature and the web.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check this week whether your university has an All of Us DURA, and apply.
3. Register on the UK Biobank and DPUK portals so you can submit once UK Biobank reopens. Whitehall II is useful as a second wrist cohort to replicate your UK Biobank results.

The interactive comparison page is at `/private/tmp/e-IgJsbM/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device, wear | N | Outcomes | Checked |

graders.name: 01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometer
graders.evidence:
Six datasets meet your requirements. The biggest finding is about UK Biobank, the standard reference cohort for wrist-outcome studies: since a data incident in April 2026 **it is not accepting new applications**. Its apply page (seen through web search) says it intends to "accept new applications in late 2026", and no firm date has been announced. You can start on NHANES today, and All of Us within days.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a wrist-worn accelerometer or tracker, worn in daily life for about 4–7+ days, in a few thousand adults or more, linked to outcomes (hospital, diagnosis or death records), and obtainable from a US university.
- **Nice to have:** sleep measured too, and raw or minute-level signal so you can compute the same metrics as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** you are willing to wait weeks to months for an application.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist data | N | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + NCHS Linked Mortality File | Open download; restricted extensions need an NCHS Research Data Center (RDC) project | Non-dominant wrist, 7 days, raw 80 Hz + minute-level | ~14,700 wearers (~7,000 adults in mortality analyses) | Deaths (public file); hospital/Medicare via restricted linkage | today |
| 2 | All of Us (Fitbit + electronic health records) | Institutional agreement (DURA) + training, days | Fitbit, months to years, summaries only | ~13–16k sharing Fitbit data; ~53k with a device record | Health-record diagnoses, visits, deaths | today |
| 3 | UK Biobank accelerometer study | Application + fee (£3,000 / 3 yrs; £500 for students), **applications paused** | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days, raw | ~100k | Hospital records, cancer, deaths, GP records | today (via search snippets) |
| 4 | Whitehall II, 2012–13 wave | Application via the DPUK portal, weeks; fee possibly £500 | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days, raw | 4,204 | Hospital records + mortality (linkage from memory) | today (via search snippets) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank accelerometer study | Application, £2,500 per request outside China | Axivity AX3, wrist (2020–21) | ~20,400 | Insurance claims + deaths (from memory); short follow-up | partly; release status unconfirmed |
| 6 | MrOS + SOF actigraphy | Free registration (from memory) | SleepWatch-O, non-dominant wrist, 4–5 days, 1-min counts | ~3,000 men + ~3,000 women, aged 65+ | Deaths, fractures, cardiovascular events confirmed by the studies | sizes/device today; access from memory |

## Details and how to get each one
1. **NHANES 2011–2014** ([PAXMIN_G docs](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/Nchs/Data/Nhanes/Public/2011/DataFiles/PAXMIN_G.htm), [mortality linkage](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/linked-data/mortality-files/)).
   - **Data:** about 99% of monitors were on the non-dominant wrist. Files include a minute-by-minute wake/sleep/non-wear prediction (`PAXPREDM`), and the raw 80 Hz data is about 1 TB compressed.
   - **Get it:** download the accelerometer files and the public-use mortality file directly. The public mortality file comes from an earlier linkage and has altered details. Follow-up to 2022 and the Medicare linkage are only in restricted files at an NCHS Research Data Center, which needs a project application.
   - **Extra files:** activity counts and step counts per minute for all 14,693 wearers are on [PhysioNet](https://physionet.org/content/minute-level-step-count-nhanes/1.0.2/) (CC0, open).
   - **Example paper:** an [activity fragmentation and mortality study](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-026-29778-9) (2026).
   - Use the survey weights.
2. **All of Us** ([access tiers](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/data-access/)).
   - **Get it:** your institution's signing official signs the DURA (many US universities already have). You then register, verify your identity and complete the research conduct training. Controlled-tier data (including deaths) needs extra training.
   - **Caveats:** Fitbit gives proprietary summaries, not raw acceleration, so comparing with raw-signal wrist studies is limited. People who share Fitbit data are a self-selected group. Analysis is cloud-only.
   - **Example papers:** [Nature Medicine 2022 on step counts and chronic disease](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-022-02012-w), and [a 2026 Circulation: Cardiovascular Quality and Outcomes paper on sleep](https://doi.org/10.1161/circoutcomes.126.014445).
3. **UK Biobank** ([apply](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/apply-for-access/), [fees](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/)).
   - **Why it matters:** this is the reference dataset most other wrist studies use, so it's the best one for comparability.
   - **Status:** its analysis platform was suspended on 23 April 2026. Reopening reportedly waits on government approval, exporting results files will at first be restricted, and new GP data is being withheld for now.
   - **Get it:** register in the Access Management System now and watch the UK Biobank Community site for the reopening date.
   - **Example papers:** [Doherty 2017](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0169649) and [activity and 697 diseases (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-022-00676-9).
4. **Whitehall II** ([data-sharing FAQ](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/brain-sciences/psychiatry/our-research/mental-health-older-people/whitehall-ii/data-sharing/data-sharing-faq)).

graders.name: 02-recall-nhanes-wrist
graders.evidence:
Six datasets meet your requirements. The biggest finding is about UK Biobank, the standard reference cohort for wrist-outcome studies: since a data incident in April 2026 **it is not accepting new applications**. Its apply page (seen through web search) says it intends to "accept new applications in late 2026", and no firm date has been announced. You can start on NHANES today, and All of Us within days.

## What I assumed you need

- **Nice to have:** sleep measured too, and raw or minute-level signal so you can compute the same metrics as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** you are willing to wait weeks to months for an application.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist data | N | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + NCHS Linked Mortality File | Open download; restricted extensions need an NCHS Research Data Center (RDC) project | Non-dominant wrist, 7 days, raw 80 Hz + minute-level | ~14,700 wearers (~7,000 adults in mortality analyses) | Deaths (public file); hospital/Medicare via restricted linkage | today |
| 2 | All of Us (Fitbit + electronic health records) | Institutional agreement (DURA) + training, days | Fitbit, months to years, summaries only | ~13–16k sharing Fitbit data; ~53k with a device record | Health-record diagnoses, visits, deaths | today |
| 3 | UK Biobank accelerometer study | Application + fee (£3,000 / 3 yrs; £500 for students), **applications paused** | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days, raw | ~100k | Hospital records, cancer, deaths, GP records | today (via search snippets) |
| 4 | Whitehall II, 2012–13 wave | Application via the DPUK portal, weeks; fee possibly £500 | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days, raw | 4,204 | Hospital records + mortality (linkage from memory) | today (via search snippets) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank accelerometer study | Application, £2,500 per request outside China | Axivity AX3, wrist (2020–21) | ~20,400 | Insurance claims + deaths (from memory); short follow-up | partly; release status unconfirmed |
| 6 | MrOS + SOF actigraphy | Free registration (from memory) | SleepWatch-O, non-dominant wrist, 4–5 days, 1-min counts | ~3,000 men + ~3,000 women, aged 65+ | Deaths, fractures, cardiovascular events confirmed by the studies | sizes/device today; access from memory |

graders.name: 05-access-allofus-dura
graders.evidence:
Six datasets meet your requirements. The biggest finding is about UK Biobank, the standard reference cohort for wrist-outcome studies: since a data incident in April 2026 **it is not accepting new applications**. Its apply page (seen through web search) says it intends to "accept new applications in late 2026", and no firm date has been announced. You can start on NHANES today, and All of Us within days.

## What I assumed you need

- **Nice to have:** sleep measured too, and raw or minute-level signal so you can compute the same metrics as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** you are willing to wait weeks to months for an application.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist data | N | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + NCHS Linked Mortality File | Open download; restricted extensions need an NCHS Research Data Center (RDC) project | Non-dominant wrist, 7 days, raw 80 Hz + minute-level | ~14,700 wearers (~7,000 adults in mortality analyses) | Deaths (public file); hospital/Medicare via restricted linkage | today |
| 2 | All of Us (Fitbit + electronic health records) | Institutional agreement (DURA) + training, days | Fitbit, months to years, summaries only | ~13–16k sharing Fitbit data; ~53k with a device record | Health-record diagnoses, visits, deaths | today |
| 3 | UK Biobank accelerometer study | Application + fee (£3,000 / 3 yrs; £500 for students), **applications paused** | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days, raw | ~100k | Hospital records, cancer, deaths, GP records | today (via search snippets) |
| 4 | Whitehall II, 2012–13 wave | Application via the DPUK portal, weeks; fee possibly £500 | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days, raw | 4,204 | Hospital records + mortality (linkage from memory) | today (via search snippets) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank accelerometer study | Application, £2,500 per request outside China | Axivity AX3, wrist (2020–21) | ~20,400 | Insurance claims + deaths (from memory); short follow-up | partly; release status unconfirmed |
| 6 | MrOS + SOF actigraphy | Free registration (from memory) | SleepWatch-O, non-dominant wrist, 4–5 days, 1-min counts | ~3,000 men + ~3,000 women, aged 65+ | Deaths, fractures, cardiovascular events confirmed by the studies | sizes/device today; access from memory |

## Details and how to get each one

2. **All of Us** ([access tiers](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/data-access/)).

The biggest finding is about UK Biobank, the standard reference cohort for wrist-outcome studies: since a data incident in April 2026 **it is not accepting new applications**. | 2 | All of Us (Fitbit + electronic health records) | Institutional agreement (DURA) + training, days | Fitbit, months to years, summaries only | ~13–16k sharing Fitbit data; ~53k with a device record | Health-record diagnoses, visits, deaths | today |
| 3 | UK Biobank accelerometer study | Application + fee (£3,000 / 3 yrs; £500 for students), **applications paused** | Axivity AX3, dominant wrist, 7 days, raw | ~100k | Hospital records, cancer, deaths, GP records | today (via search snippets) |
| 4 | Whitehall II, 2012–13 wave | Application via the DPUK portal, weeks; fee possibly £500 | GENEActiv, non-dominant wrist, 9 days, raw | 4,204 | Hospital records + mortality (linkage from memory) | today (via search snippets) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank accelerometer study | Application, £2,500 per request outside China | Axivity AX3, wrist (2020–21) | ~20,400 | Insurance claims + deaths (from memory); short follow-up | partly; release status unconfirmed |
| 6 | MrOS + SOF actigraphy | Free registration (from memory) | SleepWatch-O, non-dominant wrist, 4–5 days, 1-min counts | ~3,000 men + ~3,000 women, aged 65+ | Deaths, fractures, cardiovascular events confirmed by the studies | sizes/device today; access from memory |

graders.name: 01-recall-ukbiobank-accelerometer
graders.evidence:
I found eight datasets worth considering. The one most wrist studies compare against, **UK Biobank, is not taking new applications right now**. **NHANES 2011–2014 is the one you can start on today**, and **All of Us** is likely the fastest route to records-linked data for a US university.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** a wrist-worn device; several days or more of everyday wear; a few thousand adults or more; linked outcomes (hospital records, diagnoses or deaths).
- **Nice to have:** raw or minute-level signal, so you can process it the same way as other wrist studies.
- **Assumed:** non-US cohorts are fine, and waiting weeks to months for approval is acceptable.

## Shortlist (checked 12 Nov 2026)
| # | Dataset | Access | Wrist device / size | Outcomes | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NHANES 2011–14 + Linked Mortality Files | Direct download; minutes | ActiGraph GT3X+, 9 days, ~12,600–14,700 | Deaths only (to 2019 public; to 2022 restricted) | today |
| 2 | UK Biobank accelerometer sub-study | Application + fee; **new applications paused** | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~100k | Hospital records, deaths, cancer | today (web search) |
| 3 | All of Us (Fitbit + health records) | Institutional agreement + training; days | Fitbit, often months, 12.8k in 2022 (more now) | Health-record diagnoses | today |
| 4 | Whitehall II (GENEActiv) | Application via Dementias Platform UK; weeks | GENEActiv, 9 days, 4,204 | Deaths; hospital records from memory | today (web search) |
| 5 | China Kadoorie Biobank, 3rd resurvey | Application; months; release status unclear | Axivity AX3, 7 days, ~20,400 | Hospital insurance and death registries (from memory); short follow-up | today (web search) |
| 6 | MrOS (older men) | Free registration + online agreement; days | Wrist actigraph, ~5 nights, 3,135 | Reviewed deaths and heart events, ~15 yrs | today (web search) |
| 7 | MESA Sleep | Agreement + ethics approval (IRB); weeks | Actiwatch, 7 days, 2,237 | Heart events via a separate request | today (web search) |
| 8 | Rush Memory and Aging Project | Data request; weeks | Actical, up to 10 days, repeated, ~1,000+ | Deaths, dementia, autopsy | today (web search) |

"Today" means I confirmed the page with the checking tool. "Today (web search)" means the site blocked automated checks (UK Biobank, UCL, CKB, UCSF, sleepdata.org and Rush all did), so those facts come from web search results today, not from the site itself.

## Details and access steps
**1. NHANES 2011–2014.** Participants wore an ActiGraph on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days, and minute-level files (in MIMS units) are released.
- **Access:** download the activity files for the 2011–12 and 2013–14 cycles, then the public mortality files from the [CDC linked-data page](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm). No application.
- **Limits:** the public files end follow-up on 31 Dec 2019, and CDC alters follow-up time or cause of death for a few records to protect privacy. Follow-up to 2022 is only available as restricted files through an NCHS Research Data Center, which takes months.
- **Outcomes:** deaths only, no hospital records.
- **Example paper:** [PMC11402588](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/).

**2. UK Biobank.** Still the best match on paper: about 100k adults, raw 100 Hz signal, and linked hospital, cancer and death records.
- **Status:** its FAQ (updated 22 Oct 2026) says "We are not currently accepting applications for new research projects", with reopening planned for late 2026. This follows a [data leak in 2026](https://www.the-scientist.com/uk-biobank-to-restore-access-months-after-massive-data-leak-75197).
- **Fees when it reopens:** Tier 1 is £3,000 for 3 years (£500 for students, who must apply with their supervisor). See the [fees page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/).
- **Where you analyse:** only on its cloud platform (UKB-RAP), with compute billed separately. Some new linked health data is being held back until government data providers sign off.
- **Plan for now:** register on its application system and prepare your proposal.
- **Example paper:** [10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213).

**3. All of Us.**
- **Access:** your university must have signed a Data Use and Registration Agreement (most large US universities have). You then register on the [Researcher Workbench](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), verify your identity and complete training. The Controlled Tier, which has real event dates, needs an amended agreement and extra training.
- **Rules:** you work only in their cloud workbench and may not link records to outside data.
- **Caveat for comparability:** this is consumer-tracker output (steps, heart rate, sleep stages), not raw acceleration. People who already own a Fitbit are also not a random sample.
- **Recent papers:** many on sleep, activity and disease.

**4. Whitehall II.** About 4,200 participants wore a GENEActiv on the non-dominant wrist for 9 days in 2012–13.
- **Access:** apply through the [DPUK portal](https://portal.dementiasplatform.uk/data/cohort-data-availability/). You choose variables, the Whitehall committee reviews the request, you sign an access agreement and you analyse in a secure remote environment.
- **To ask:** whether the raw device files are available (whitehall2@ucl.ac.uk).

**5. China Kadoorie Biobank.** The same device as UK Biobank, worn by about 20,000 adults in 2020–21 ([Chen et al. 2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8)).
- **Status:** I could not confirm whether the accelerometer data has been released to researchers through the CKB Data Access System yet.
- **Limit:** follow-up is still short.

**6. MrOS.** Free registration and an online data-use agreement on MrOS Online. It has actigraphy from the sleep visit (n=3,135) and mortality with more than half of participants deceased. See this [mortality paper](https://academic.oup.com/sleep/article/45/4/zsac015/6509372). The sister study of older women, SOF (about 3,000), is requested through SOF Online, and its access terms are not confirmed.

**7. MESA Sleep.** Raw actigraphy is on the National Sleep Research Resource (NSRR), which needs a data-use agreement and ethics approval (IRB). Heart events must be requested separately from BioLINCC or the MESA Coordinating Center.

**8. Rush Memory and Aging Project.** Request through the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center (RADC) Research Resource Sharing Hub. It is smaller than your target, but people wore the device repeatedly over years.

## Known, not confirmed
- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended
These wore the device on the hip or thigh, which fails your wrist requirement:
- NHANES 2003–06, the Women's Health Study and the WHI OPACH study (hip)
- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
- REGARDS, Tromsø 7 and the German National Cohort (hip, from memory)
- 1970 British Cohort Study (thigh)

These are wrist-based but probably fall short:
- HCHS/SOL Sueño: about 1,900 participants on NSRR, and published work so far does not follow people over time.
- Rotterdam Study (GENEActiv): about 1,200–1,400 people, requested by email.

## What I could not find
No openly downloadable wrist dataset that is also linked to hospital records. NHANES has deaths only.

## Next step
1. Start on NHANES now.
2. Check whether your university has an All of Us agreement, and register.
3. Draft a UK Biobank application for when it reopens.
4. Email the Whitehall II team about the raw device files.

Pooling NHANES or All of Us with UK Biobank and Whitehall II would give you external validation on different wrist devices.

I've saved an interactive version of this shortlist, where you can filter, compare datasets and export an access plan: `/private/tmp/e-Dth5Qj/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

Sources: [UK Biobank fees](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/fees/), [UK Biobank apply page](https://www.ukbiobank.ac.uk/use-our-data/apply-for-access/), [The Scientist](https://www.the-scientist.com/uk-biobank-to-restore-access-months-after-massive-data-leak-75197), [CDC public mortality files](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data-linkage/mortality-public.htm), [CDC linked-data FTP](https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/Health_Statistics/NCHS/datalinkage/linked_mortality/), [NHANES mortality paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11402588/), [All of Us Workbench](https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/workbench/), [All of Us data access framework](https://support.researchallofus.org/hc/en-us/articles/22346942074132-Data-Access-Framework), [DPUK cohort availability](https://portal.dementiasplatform.uk/data/cohort-data-availability/), [Whitehall II data sharing](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/brain-sciences/psychiatry/our-research/mental-health-older-people/whitehall-ii/data-sharing), [CKB resurvey](https://www.ckbiobank.org/news-1/3rd-resurvey-of-ckb-participants-completed), [CKB accelerometry paper](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12966-023-01537-8), [MrOS Online](https://sfcc.ucsf.edu/news/over-16-years-prospective-data-mros-online), [NSRR MrOS](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mros), [NSRR MESA](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/mesa), [NSRR HCHS/SOL](https://sleepdata.org/datasets/hchs), [RADC study designs](https://www.radc.rush.edu/docs/parentStudyDesigns.htm), [Rotterdam wrist accelerometry paper](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5739112/)

- The device MrOS used (from memory: SleepWatch-O, a wrist actigraph), and whether raw epochs are available.
- Whitehall II's hospital-record linkage (from memory).
- Two smaller US cohorts I did not check: the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (wrist ActiGraph/GENEActiv, roughly 1,000 people, application at blsa.nih.gov) and the Study of Osteoporotic Fractures (SOF).

## Not recommended

- HUNT4 (thigh and lower back)
