graders.name: 01-recall-ami-meetings
graders.evidence:
For data you can use commercially and download today, start with **NOTSOFAR-1** and **AMI**, both CC BY 4.0. Add **CHiME-6**, **ICSI** and **DiPCo** for more variety, and **Earnings-21/22** if you want real business speech that isn't far-field. Together these come to roughly 250–300 hours. Every licence below was checked against the official source on 2026-11-12, unless it's marked "from memory".

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** real multi-party conversation, ideally business meetings. I counted AMI's role-play design meetings as real, because the talk itself is unscripted.
- **R2 (must):** speaker-turn labels (who spoke when).
- **R3 (nice to have):** far-field or microphone-array audio.
- **R4 (must):** English.
- **R5 (must):** commercial use allowed. A fee is fine; non-commercial or "research only" is out. I took "commercial use" to include training models that you then ship.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NOTSOFAR-1 (recorded meetings) | Open download | CC BY 4.0 | 237 meetings of about 6 min each, several devices per meeting | Strong | today |
| 2 | AMI Meeting Corpus | Open download | CC BY 4.0 | About 100 h | Strong | today (size from memory) |
| 3 | CHiME-6 (dinner parties) | Open download, about 120 GB | CC BY-SA 4.0 | About 40 h (from memory) | Strong for far-field, but not business | today |
| 4 | ICSI Meeting Corpus (Edinburgh release) | Open download | CC BY 4.0 | About 70 h | Partial: no far-field audio in this release | today |
| 5 | DiPCo (Amazon) | Open download | CDLA-Permissive-1.0 | About 5 h (from memory) | Partial: small, not business | today |
| 6 | Earnings-21 / Earnings-22 (Rev) | Open download (GitHub, Git LFS) | CC BY-SA 4.0 | 39 h, plus about 119 h for E-22 (from memory) | Partial: phone/webcast audio | today |
| 7 | LDC meeting sets: ICSI with far-field channels (LDC2004S02), NIST RT-05S, ISL | Paid: LDC for-profit membership, takes weeks | LDC membership agreement | Small | Partial | today (fees from memory) |

## Details
1. **NOTSOFAR-1** (github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge; data at huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/NOTSOFAR)
   - **Contents:** the README describes "237 meetings… recorded across 30 conference rooms with 4-8 attendees", recorded on both single-channel and multi-channel far-field devices, with ground-truth labels. This is the closest match to your product.
   - **Licence:** the README says "licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License".
   - **Get it:** call `download_meeting_subset()` from the repo.
   - **Watch out for:**
     - Only 35 unique speakers, so speaker variety is low.
     - The same README calls the data "provided for open research". The licence it states is still CC BY 4.0, but get a quick legal read.
     - Leave out the ~1000 h simulated training set if you only want real audio.
   - **Used in:** the Interspeech 2024 dataset paper (doi:10.21437/interspeech.2024-1788) and the BUT/JHU CHiME-8 system (doi:10.21437/chime.2024-4).
2. **AMI** (groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/)
   - **Licence:** the licence page says "The AMI corpus and its annotations are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license".
   - **Contents (from memory):** headset, lapel and two 8-mic circular arrays, with speaker-aligned transcripts.
   - **Watch out for:** about two thirds are role-play design-team meetings. Many speakers are non-native.
   - **Used in:** the corpus paper (doi:10.1007/s10579-007-9040-x).
3. **CHiME-6** (openslr.org/150)
   - **Licence:** OpenSLR lists "License: Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0". This is the current release; CHiME-5 originally had a more restrictive licence, so make sure you take this one.
   - **Contents:** real 4-person dinner parties recorded on distributed Kinect arrays, with JSON transcripts carrying speaker IDs and times. There is a lot of overlapping speech.
   - **Watch out for:** ShareAlike means any modified dataset you share must stay CC BY-SA. Whether trained model weights count is a question for your lawyer.
   - **Used in:** the CHiME-8 DASR overview (doi:10.21437/chime.2024-1).
4. **ICSI, Edinburgh release** (groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/)
   - **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, confirmed on the page.
   - **Contents:** real research-group meetings.
   - **Watch out for:** the download page only offers "Headset mix" and "Individual channel headsets". From memory, the tabletop distant mics are only in the LDC version (#7).
5. **DiPCo** (zenodo.org/records/8122551)
   - **Contents:** real conversations between "four Amazon employee volunteers", recorded with close-talk mics and "five far-field 7-microphone" arrays.
   - **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive-1.0, which allows commercial use.
   - **Best use:** a small, clean far-field evaluation set.
6. **Earnings-21/22** (github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets)
   - **Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0.
   - **Contents:** real business calls with a speaker ID on every word.
   - **Check:** whether the `ts`/`endTs` timing columns are filled in. If not, you'll need forced alignment to get turn times.
   - **Watch out for:** no far-field audio, and less overlap than real meetings.
7. **LDC (paid route).** I confirmed this on LDC's licensing page today:
   - Non-members, including for-profit companies, "cannot use LDC data… for any commercial purpose".
   - For-profit members get commercial rights to the data they license during their membership year.
   - So buying a single corpus without joining does **not** give you commercial rights; you have to join.
   - From memory, for-profit membership has cost tens of thousands of USD a year. Ask the LDC Membership Office for current fees.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Commercial data vendors** such as Appen, Defined.ai and Shaip. From memory, they sell off-the-shelf meeting audio or collect it to order with diarization labels and commercial licences. I didn't check any of them. If you need hundreds of hours of varied, consented business meetings recorded on devices like yours, this is probably the only route.

## Not recommended, and why
- **VoxConverse:** the README says "for research purposes", and the audio comes from YouTube. It's also broadcast content, not meetings.
- **MeetingBank and ground-truth/multichannel-meetings-10h:** non-commercial licences (NC).
- **Simulated or replayed audio** (NOTSOFAR simulated set, LibriCSS, LibriWASN): you've ruled these out.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** Mandarin.
- **DIHARD, Fisher, Switchboard, CALLHOME, Mixer 6:** these come from LDC (so membership is needed for commercial use), and most are 2-party phone calls or interviews.
- **Unofficial Hugging Face mirrors of ICSI and DiPCo:** use the official sources instead.

## What I could not find
I found no large (hundreds of hours), recent, real English business-meeting corpus with array audio and a commercial licence. The open sets above are the whole public supply. The literature search added little, because the speech conference venues are poorly indexed in the sources the tool uses.

## Next step
1. Download NOTSOFAR-1 and AMI today and set up your diarization benchmark: DER on NOTSOFAR, AMI and DiPCo.
2. Have counsel sign off on two things: CC BY-SA for CHiME-6 and Earnings, and the NOTSOFAR "open research" wording.
3. Then decide whether to scale up with a vendor collection or with LDC membership.

The interactive shortlist, with filters and an access-plan export, is at `/private/tmp/e-55YarO/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

graders.name: 02-recall-chime6-dinner-party
graders.evidence:
For data you can use commercially and download today, start with **NOTSOFAR-1** and **AMI**, both CC BY 4.0. Add **CHiME-6**, **ICSI** and **DiPCo** for more variety, and **Earnings-21/22** if you want real business speech that isn't far-field. Together these come to roughly 250–300 hours. Every licence below was checked against the official source on 2026-11-12, unless it's marked "from memory".

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** real multi-party conversation, ideally business meetings. I counted AMI's role-play design meetings as real, because the talk itself is unscripted.
- **R2 (must):** speaker-turn labels (who spoke when).
- **R3 (nice to have):** far-field or microphone-array audio.
- **R4 (must):** English.
- **R5 (must):** commercial use allowed. A fee is fine; non-commercial or "research only" is out. I took "commercial use" to include training models that you then ship.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NOTSOFAR-1 (recorded meetings) | Open download | CC BY 4.0 | 237 meetings of about 6 min each, several devices per meeting | Strong | today |
| 2 | AMI Meeting Corpus | Open download | CC BY 4.0 | About 100 h | Strong | today (size from memory) |
| 3 | CHiME-6 (dinner parties) | Open download, about 120 GB | CC BY-SA 4.0 | About 40 h (from memory) | Strong for far-field, but not business | today |
| 4 | ICSI Meeting Corpus (Edinburgh release) | Open download | CC BY 4.0 | About 70 h | Partial: no far-field audio in this release | today |
| 5 | DiPCo (Amazon) | Open download | CDLA-Permissive-1.0 | About 5 h (from memory) | Partial: small, not business | today |
| 6 | Earnings-21 / Earnings-22 (Rev) | Open download (GitHub, Git LFS) | CC BY-SA 4.0 | 39 h, plus about 119 h for E-22 (from memory) | Partial: phone/webcast audio | today |
| 7 | LDC meeting sets: ICSI with far-field channels (LDC2004S02), NIST RT-05S, ISL | Paid: LDC for-profit membership, takes weeks | LDC membership agreement | Small | Partial | today (fees from memory) |

## Details
1. **NOTSOFAR-1** (github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge; data at huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/NOTSOFAR)
   - **Contents:** the README describes "237 meetings… recorded across 30 conference rooms with 4-8 attendees", recorded on both single-channel and multi-channel far-field devices, with ground-truth labels. This is the closest match to your product.
   - **Licence:** the README says "licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License".
   - **Get it:** call `download_meeting_subset()` from the repo.
   - **Watch out for:**
     - Only 35 unique speakers, so speaker variety is low.
     - The same README calls the data "provided for open research". The licence it states is still CC BY 4.0, but get a quick legal read.
     - Leave out the ~1000 h simulated training set if you only want real audio.
   - **Used in:** the Interspeech 2024 dataset paper (doi:10.21437/interspeech.2024-1788) and the BUT/JHU CHiME-8 system (doi:10.21437/chime.2024-4).
2. **AMI** (groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/)
   - **Licence:** the licence page says "The AMI corpus and its annotations are released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license".
   - **Contents (from memory):** headset, lapel and two 8-mic circular arrays, with speaker-aligned transcripts.
   - **Watch out for:** about two thirds are role-play design-team meetings. Many speakers are non-native.
   - **Used in:** the corpus paper (doi:10.1007/s10579-007-9040-x).
3. **CHiME-6** (openslr.org/150)
   - **Licence:** OpenSLR lists "License: Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0". This is the current release; CHiME-5 originally had a more restrictive licence, so make sure you take this one.
   - **Contents:** real 4-person dinner parties recorded on distributed Kinect arrays, with JSON transcripts carrying speaker IDs and times. There is a lot of overlapping speech.
   - **Watch out for:** ShareAlike means any modified dataset you share must stay CC BY-SA. Whether trained model weights count is a question for your lawyer.
   - **Used in:** the CHiME-8 DASR overview (doi:10.21437/chime.2024-1).
4. **ICSI, Edinburgh release** (groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/)
   - **Licence:** CC BY 4.0, confirmed on the page.
   - **Contents:** real research-group meetings.
   - **Watch out for:** the download page only offers "Headset mix" and "Individual channel headsets". From memory, the tabletop distant mics are only in the LDC version (#7).
5. **DiPCo** (zenodo.org/records/8122551)
   - **Contents:** real conversations between "four Amazon employee volunteers", recorded with close-talk mics and "five far-field 7-microphone" arrays.
   - **Licence:** CDLA-Permissive-1.0, which allows commercial use.
   - **Best use:** a small, clean far-field evaluation set.
6. **Earnings-21/22** (github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets)
   - **Licence:** CC BY-SA 4.0.
   - **Contents:** real business calls with a speaker ID on every word.
   - **Check:** whether the `ts`/`endTs` timing columns are filled in. If not, you'll need forced alignment to get turn times.
   - **Watch out for:** no far-field audio, and less overlap than real meetings.
7. **LDC (paid route).** I confirmed this on LDC's licensing page today:
   - Non-members, including for-profit companies, "cannot use LDC data… for any commercial purpose".
   - For-profit members get commercial rights to the data they license during their membership year.
   - So buying a single corpus without joining does **not** give you commercial rights; you have to join.
   - From memory, for-profit membership has cost tens of thousands of USD a year. Ask the LDC Membership Office for current fees.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Commercial data vendors** such as Appen, Defined.ai and Shaip. From memory, they sell off-the-shelf meeting audio or collect it to order with diarization labels and commercial licences. I didn't check any of them. If you need hundreds of hours of varied, consented business meetings recorded on devices like yours, this is probably the only route.

## Not recommended, and why
- **VoxConverse:** the README says "for research purposes", and the audio comes from YouTube. It's also broadcast content, not meetings.
- **MeetingBank and ground-truth/multichannel-meetings-10h:** non-commercial licences (NC).
- **Simulated or replayed audio** (NOTSOFAR simulated set, LibriCSS, LibriWASN): you've ruled these out.
- **AliMeeting and AISHELL-4:** Mandarin.
- **DIHARD, Fisher, Switchboard, CALLHOME, Mixer 6:** these come from LDC (so membership is needed for commercial use), and most are 2-party phone calls or interviews.
- **Unofficial Hugging Face mirrors of ICSI and DiPCo:** use the official sources instead.

## What I could not find
I found no large (hundreds of hours), recent, real English business-meeting corpus with array audio and a commercial licence. The open sets above are the whole public supply. The literature search added little, because the speech conference venues are poorly indexed in the sources the tool uses.

## Next step
1. Download NOTSOFAR-1 and AMI today and set up your diarization benchmark: DER on NOTSOFAR, AMI and DiPCo.
2. Have counsel sign off on two things: CC BY-SA for CHiME-6 and Earnings, and the NOTSOFAR "open research" wording.
3. Then decide whether to scale up with a vendor collection or with LDC membership.

The interactive shortlist, with filters and an access-plan export, is at `/private/tmp/e-55YarO/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

graders.name: 01-recall-ami-meetings
graders.evidence:
Use **AMI** and **NOTSOFAR-1** first. Both are real English meetings with speaker-attributed transcripts and microphone-array audio, under CC BY 4.0, which allows commercial use. You can download both today. If you want more data later, a paid LDC for-profit membership is the main way to add more.

Checked on 12 Nov 2026 against each dataset's official pages unless marked "from memory".

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** real (not simulated) multi-party conversation; who-spoke-when labels; English; a licence that allows commercial use (a fee is fine).
- **Nice to have:** business-style meetings; far-field or microphone-array audio.
- **Assumed:** "Commercial use" means training and evaluating models for a product. You don't need to redistribute the raw data.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [AMI Meeting Corpus](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/download/) | Direct download, minutes | CC BY 4.0 | ~100 h, 2 tabletop 8-mic arrays + headsets | Strong | today |
| 2 | [NOTSOFAR-1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/NOTSOFAR) ([repo](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge)) | Direct download, no sign-up | CC BY 4.0 | 315 office meetings, 30 rooms, up to 7 far-field devices | Strong | today |
| 3 | [ICSI Meeting Corpus (free Edinburgh release)](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/) | Direct download | CC BY 4.0 | ~72 h | Partial: headset audio only | today |
| 4 | [DiPCo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551) | Direct download | CDLA-Permissive 1.0 | 10 sessions, 4 speakers each, 5 arrays | Partial: dinner parties | today |
| 5 | [CHiME-6 (OpenSLR 150)](https://openslr.org/150/) | Direct download, ~120 GB | CC BY-SA 4.0 | ~40 h, 6 Kinect arrays | Partial: dinner parties | today |
| 6 | [ICSI Meeting Speech, LDC2004S02](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S02) | LDC for-profit membership, weeks | LDC commercial licence | ICSI including far-field mics | Strong | today (terms); far-field contents from memory |
| 7 | [NIST RT-05S eval set, LDC2011S06](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2011S06) (+ RT-06S/07S) | LDC for-profit membership | LDC | Small benchmark sets | Partial | today (catalog); contents partly from memory |
| 8 | [NIST Meeting Pilot, LDC2004S09](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S09) | LDC for-profit membership | LDC | ~15 h | Partial | catalog today; details from memory |
| 9 | [ISL Meeting Speech, LDC2004S05](https://catalog.ldc.upenn.edu/LDC2004S05) | LDC for-profit membership | LDC | — | Partial | catalog today |
| 10 | [Rev Earnings-21](https://github.com/revdotcom/speech-datasets) | git clone (LFS) | CC BY-SA 4.0 (transcripts) | ~39 h | Weak: calls, not far-field | today |

## Details
**1. AMI.** About two-thirds are "scenario" meetings: real people playing a product-design team, unscripted, usually 4 participants. The rest are natural meetings. The free download includes the headset audio and two tabletop microphone arrays. The download page says: *"audio channels from 2 table top microphone arrays"*. Manual word-level transcripts with speaker IDs come in NXT format, and the usual diarization references are built from them.
- **Licence:** the licence page says *"released under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license"*. You only need to give credit.
- **Steps:** download the manual annotations zip, then use the page's chooser to pick the array and headset streams. It generates a wget script.
- **Caveats:** recorded around 2005 in 3 rooms, mostly 4 speakers, many non-native speakers. The role-play is a nuance, but it is real conversation, not a simulated mixture.
- **Papers:** [Carletta 2007, corpus description](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10579-007-9040-x); [Speaker diarization for meeting room audio, 2009](https://doi.org/10.21437/interspeech.2009-271).

**2. NOTSOFAR-1 (Microsoft).** Real office meetings with 4–8 attendees, recorded on commercial far-field devices: 4 tabletop devices with 7-mic arrays and 3 linear devices that give a single processed channel. It was used for the CHiME-8 distant diarization and speech recognition task.
- **Licence:** I read the repo's DATA_LICENSE file today. It is plain CC BY 4.0 with no commercial restriction. The Hugging Face dataset is not gated.
- **Caveats:** only 35 unique speakers, and meetings average about 6 minutes.
  - The 1000-hour training set is **simulated**, so use only the recorded meetings.
  - The repo says Dev-set-2 was approved only for use within the challenge.
- **Papers:** [NOTSOFAR-1 dataset paper, Interspeech 2024](https://doi.org/10.21437/interspeech.2024-1788); [BUT/JHU CHiME-8 system](https://doi.org/10.21437/chime.2024-4).

**3. ICSI (Edinburgh).** Natural weekly research meetings with 3–10 people, released under CC BY 4.0. The download page lists only *"Headset mix"* and *"Individual channel headsets"*, so the free release has **no far-field audio**. I believe the transcripts carry speaker-timed segments (from memory; check the transcript files).

**4. DiPCo (Amazon).** Real, unscripted conversation among volunteers, recorded on five 7-mic arrays, under CDLA-Permissive. It is small (about 5 h) and social rather than business. Use the Zenodo record; the original AWS link has expired.

**5. CHiME-6.** Real dinner parties in homes, with JSON transcripts carrying speaker and start/end times. The OpenSLR page says *"License: Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0"*, which allows commercial use.
- **Conflict:** the old CHiME-5 terms charged commercial users £2,000. Keep the bundled LICENSE.txt and have counsel confirm.
- **ShareAlike** applies to redistributed adapted data. Whether it reaches trained models is a legal question.

**6–9. LDC meeting corpora.** LDC's non-member licence is research-only. LDC newsletters say for-profit organisations without membership *"cannot use LDC data to develop or test products for commercialization"*. Commercial use needs the [For-Profit Membership](https://www.ldc.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/for-profit-membership-agreement.pdf). An undated agreement PDF puts the Standard tier at **$24,000/year for up to 16 corpora**; ask LDC for a current quote. Membership gets you:
- the ICSI far-field (PZM tabletop) channels, from memory: 4 tabletop + 2 cheap microphones;
- the NIST RT meeting sets, which are the classic meeting-diarization benchmarks;
- the NIST Meeting Pilot and ISL meeting corpora.

**10. Earnings-21.** Real business calls with speaker IDs per word (Earnings-22 has no speaker labels). It's telephone/webcast audio dominated by presenters. CC BY-SA covers the transcripts, but the Earnings-22 paper rests the audio on fair use. Get legal review before training a product on it.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Commercial data vendors** (Appen, Defined.ai, Shaip and similar) sell or commission English meeting recordings with diarization labels and full commercial rights. I didn't check their current catalogues or prices.

## Not recommended, and why
- **EasyCom (Meta):** CC BY-NC 4.0, so non-commercial.
- **ELITR Minuting Corpus:** text only (no audio), and reported as CC BY-NC-SA.
- **VoxConverse:** YouTube debates and news, not meetings. Its page says the audio is *"currently not available on this website"*, and the audio rights belong to the YouTube creators.
- **LibriCSS and other simulated mixtures:** you excluded these.
- **AliMeeting, AISHELL-4, MISP-Meeting:** Mandarin.
- **SPGISpeech:** non-commercial licence (from memory).
- **DIHARD III, Mixer 6 (LDC):** mostly not meetings. Consider them only if you already hold an LDC membership.

## What I could not find
- No free, commercially licensed corpus of real **business** meetings with arrays is larger than about 100 h (AMI). NOTSOFAR-1 is the most realistic but small.
- For production-scale training you will probably need to commission or buy data, or record your own customers' meetings with consent.

The registry searches were noisy, and the Hugging Face search partly failed. LDC's fee page blocked automated access.

## Next step
1. Download AMI (arrays and annotations) and NOTSOFAR-1 today, and build your diarization training and evaluation pipeline on them.
2. Use DiPCo and CHiME-6 for far-field robustness, after counsel confirms the CHiME-6 ShareAlike terms.
3. Ask LDC for a for-profit membership quote. It gets you ICSI far-field and the NIST RT sets as extra benchmarks.
4. Get quotes from one or two vendors for custom business-meeting recordings.

Licences and access rules change, so recheck these before you sign anything. I didn't save anything to your repo's git history. The interactive page lets you filter and compare the datasets and export an access plan.

Files are in `/private/tmp/e-FNI7jr/home/cwd`:
- `dataset-shortlist.html`
- `dataset-scout/shortlist.json`

graders.name: 01-recall-ami-meetings
graders.evidence:
I recommend building on **NOTSOFAR-1 and AMI**, adding **ICSI**, and using **DiPCo** as an extra far-field test set. I checked the licence page for each one, and all four allow commercial use with no fee. Each needs attribution, and for each I've noted what's weaker about it.

### Best fits

| Corpus | What it is | Far-field / arrays | Size | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **NOTSOFAR-1** (Microsoft, CHiME-8) | Real office meetings with 4–8 people, recorded in 30 different conference rooms | Several commercial multi-channel array devices plus single-channel devices per meeting | 237 recorded meetings averaging ~6 min, plus ~1,000 h of simulated training data | **CC BY 4.0** (confirmed in the repo's DATA_LICENSE) |
| **AMI Meeting Corpus** | Business-style meetings of about 4 people, with speaker-turn and word-level annotations | Two 8-mic circular arrays, plus headset and lapel mics | ~100 h | **CC BY 4.0** |
| **ICSI Meeting Corpus** | Real weekly research-group meetings with 3–10 people | Tabletop distant mics plus close-talk mics; no proper arrays | ~72 h | **CC BY 4.0** through the Edinburgh distribution (no LDC fee) |

How they differ:
- **NOTSOFAR-1** is the closest match to your product: real, unscripted meetings on the kind of hardware customers actually use. It's small, though. The training and dev annotations are still being upgraded, and the 1,000 h training set is simulated, which is the kind of data you said you don't want. Use the real recordings for fine-tuning and evaluation. Using the simulated set is up to you.
- **AMI** has the most real meeting audio recorded on arrays. About 70% of it is scenario meetings: real people talking spontaneously, but playing assigned roles in a made-up design project. The other ~30% are naturally occurring meetings. Many of the speakers aren't native English speakers. That's good for robustness, but keep it in mind when you evaluate.
- **ICSI** gives you real, long meetings with many speakers and lots of overlap. The recordings are older and it has no arrays.

### Useful extra
- **DiPCo** (Amazon): real 4-person dinner-party conversations recorded with five far-field 7-mic arrays plus close-talk mics. It's 10 sessions of 15–45 min each. The licence is **CDLA-Permissive 1.0**, which allows commercial use. It isn't business talk, but it's a good far-field test set. The original S3 link is dead, so get it from Zenodo (record 8122551).

### Ruled out
- **CHiME-5/6**: research-only licence.
- **MSDWild**: non-commercial.
- **AliMeeting, AISHELL-4, MISP**: Mandarin.
- **LibriCSS** and similar: simulated or replayed mixtures.
- **VoxConverse**: YouTube audio, so the rights to the audio are unclear.

### If you need more real data
The open corpora together give a few hundred hours, which may be less than you need for training. Two ways to get more:
- **LDC for-profit membership or commercial licences.** For example, the NIST Meeting Pilot Corpus (LDC2004S09). LDC licences explicitly cover commercial use for paying for-profit members. Check each corpus's terms.
- **Commercial data vendors** such as Appen, Defined.ai or Shaip. They sell or custom-collect meeting audio with diarization labels and commercial rights. Custom collection is the only way to get recordings that match your own mic setups.

### Practical notes
- CC BY and CDLA-Permissive only require attribution and keeping the licence notices. Keep an attributions file listing each dataset you use. This isn't legal advice, so have whoever handles your contracts read the licence texts before you ship.
- The participants consented to research recordings years ago. The licences allow commercial use, but if you plan to publish voice samples from these recordings in marketing material, ask your counsel first.

Sources:
- [AMI licence](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)
- [ICSI licence (Edinburgh)](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/license.shtml)
- [NOTSOFAR-1 repo](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge) and [DATA_LICENSE](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge/main/DATA_LICENSE)
- [DiPCo on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551), [DiPCo paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1909.13447), [Amazon Science blog](https://www.amazon.science/blog/amazon-releases-new-public-data-set-to-help-address-cocktail-party-problem)

graders.name: 01-recall-ami-meetings
graders.evidence:
I'd use three datasets, all licensed for commercial use and all free: **AMI**, **NOTSOFAR-1** and **ICSI**. **DiPCo** is a small fourth option for extra microphone-array audio.

| Dataset | What it is | Far-field / array audio | Speaker-turn labels | Licence (checked today) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AMI Meeting Corpus** | About 100 h of English meetings, usually 4 people. | Yes: 8-mic circular arrays, plus headset and lapel mics. | Yes: word-level timing with speaker labels. A standard diarization benchmark. | **CC BY 4.0** |
| **NOTSOFAR-1** (Microsoft) | 237 real office meetings (about 6 min each), recorded in 30 conference rooms with 4–8 attendees and 35 speakers. | Yes: several multi-channel array devices and 6–7 single-channel devices per meeting, recorded at once. | Yes, ground truth for train, dev and eval. | **CC BY 4.0** (code is MIT) |
| **ICSI Meeting Corpus** | 75 real research-group meetings, about 72 h, 3–10 people each (6 on average). | Partly: tabletop microphones, but no array. | Yes: speaker-attributed transcripts, plus dialogue-act and topic annotations. | **CC BY 4.0** (free from Edinburgh; LDC also sells the transcripts) |
| **DiPCo** (Amazon) | 10 dinner-party sessions with 4 people each, about 5 h total. | Yes: five 7-mic array devices. | Yes. | **CDLA-Permissive 1.0** |

**Suggested setup:**
- Train on AMI, ICSI and NOTSOFAR together.
- Keep NOTSOFAR's eval set and AMI's standard test split for testing. NOTSOFAR's eval set is the closest match to the conference-room device audio your product will get.
- Use DiPCo for extra array audio, but it is casual conversation, not business meetings.

**Things to watch:**
- **AMI is mostly role-play.** About two-thirds of its meetings are "scenario" meetings, where real people act out a product-design project. The audio is genuinely multi-party, not artificially mixed, but the content is staged. The remaining third are natural meetings. Decide whether the staged part fits what you mean by "real".
- **NOTSOFAR licence details.**
  - Use the Hugging Face / GitHub release (DATA_LICENSE file), which is CC BY 4.0.
  - Don't use **Dev-set-2**. It was taken out of the open release and is limited to the original challenge.
  - An old CHiME-8 page still says the data is challenge-only. It's out of date, but keep a copy of the current DATA_LICENSE in your records.
  - Its roughly 1,000-hour training set is simulated. That's fine for augmentation, but it isn't the real recordings you asked for.
- **Datasets built from these may be stricter.** For example, NSF-QA, derived from NOTSOFAR, is non-commercial. Always get the original release.
- **What CC BY requires and doesn't cover.** You must credit the source. The licence also says it doesn't cover publicity or privacy rights. That's normal, but have a lawyer look at it before you ship models trained on recorded voices.
- **None of these is very large.** If you need more real business-meeting audio, the paid route is custom collection from a data vendor, or for-profit membership of the LDC, which gives access to more meeting data such as the NIST Rich Transcription sets. Check the terms for each LDC corpus yourself.

**Ruled out:** AliMeeting is Mandarin, and LibriCSS is replayed audio rather than real conversation. CHiME-5/6, Ego4D and Meta's MMCSG have research-only or restricted licences as far as I know, but I didn't re-check those today. VoxConverse is CC BY 4.0 but it's single-channel broadcast audio, so at most a secondary test set.

| Dataset | What it is | Far-field / array audio | Speaker-turn labels | Licence (checked today) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AMI Meeting Corpus** | About 100 h of English meetings, usually 4 people. | Yes: 8-mic circular arrays, plus headset and lapel mics. | Yes: word-level timing with speaker labels. A standard diarization benchmark. | **CC BY 4.0** |
| **NOTSOFAR-1** (Microsoft) | 237 real office meetings (about 6 min each), recorded in 30 conference rooms with 4–8 attendees and 35 speakers. | Yes: several multi-channel array devices and 6–7 single-channel devices per meeting, recorded at once. | Yes, ground truth for train, dev and eval. | **CC BY 4.0** (code is MIT) |
| **ICSI Meeting Corpus** | 75 real research-group meetings, about 72 h, 3–10 people each (6 on average). | Partly: tabletop microphones, but no array. | Yes: speaker-attributed transcripts, plus dialogue-act and topic annotations. | **CC BY 4.0** (free from Edinburgh; LDC also sells the transcripts) |
| **DiPCo** (Amazon) | 10 dinner-party sessions with 4 people each, about 5 h total. | Yes: five 7-mic array devices. | Yes. | **CDLA-Permissive 1.0** |

**Suggested setup:**
- Train on AMI, ICSI and NOTSOFAR together.
- Keep NOTSOFAR's eval set and AMI's standard test split for testing. NOTSOFAR's eval set is the closest match to the conference-room device audio your product will get.
- Use DiPCo for extra array audio, but it is casual conversation, not business meetings.

**Things to watch:**
- **AMI is mostly role-play.** About two-thirds of its meetings are "scenario" meetings, where real people act out a product-design project. The audio is genuinely multi-party, not artificially mixed, but the content is staged. The remaining third are natural meetings. Decide whether the staged part fits what you mean by "real".
- **NOTSOFAR licence details.**
  - Use the Hugging Face / GitHub release (DATA_LICENSE file), which is CC BY 4.0.
  - Don't use **Dev-set-2**. It was taken out of the open release and is limited to the original challenge.
  - An old CHiME-8 page still says the data is challenge-only. It's out of date, but keep a copy of the current DATA_LICENSE in your records.
  - Its roughly 1,000-hour training set is simulated. That's fine for augmentation, but it isn't the real recordings you asked for.
- **Datasets built from these may be stricter.** For example, NSF-QA, derived from NOTSOFAR, is non-commercial. Always get the original release.
- **What CC BY requires and doesn't cover.** You must credit the source. The licence also says it doesn't cover publicity or privacy rights. That's normal, but have a lawyer look at it before you ship models trained on recorded voices.
- **None of these is very large.** If you need more real business-meeting audio, the paid route is custom collection from a data vendor, or for-profit membership of the LDC, which gives access to more meeting data such as the NIST Rich Transcription sets. Check the terms for each LDC corpus yourself.

**Ruled out:** AliMeeting is Mandarin, and LibriCSS is replayed audio rather than real conversation. CHiME-5/6, Ego4D and Meta's MMCSG have research-only or restricted licences as far as I know, but I didn't re-check those today. VoxConverse is CC BY 4.0 but it's single-channel broadcast audio, so at most a secondary test set.

graders.name: 01-recall-ami-meetings
graders.evidence:
I'd build on three datasets that are free and allow commercial use: **AMI**, **NOTSOFAR-1** and **ICSI**. **DiPCo** is a useful extra, and you can pay the LDC for more if you need it. I checked the licences on the official pages today.

## Main picks

| Dataset | What it is | Far-field / arrays | Speaker-turn labels | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **AMI Meeting Corpus** | About 100 h of meetings with 3–5 people in instrumented rooms | Yes: two 8-mic circular arrays, plus headset and lapel mics | Yes: speaker segments and word-level timings | **CC BY 4.0** ([licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)) |
| **NOTSOFAR-1** (Microsoft) | Real office meetings: 237 public meetings of about 6 min each, recorded in 30 conference rooms | Yes: single-channel and multi-channel commercial meeting devices, which is very close to real deployment conditions | Yes, made for distant diarization and ASR | **CC BY 4.0** ([repo](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge)) |
| **ICSI Meeting Corpus** | About 72 h of the institute's own research meetings, not scripted | Tabletop distant mics (PZM and cheap desktop mics), plus close-talk mics | Yes: speaker-attributed transcripts with timings | **CC BY 4.0** through Edinburgh ([licence page](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/license.shtml)) |
| **DiPCo** (Amazon/JHU) | 10 dinner-party sessions with 4 people each, 15–45 min | Yes: five 7-mic far-field arrays | Yes | **CDLA-Permissive 1.0** ([Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551), the official copy now) |

**Things to watch for with each:**
- **AMI:** About two-thirds of the meetings are "scenario" meetings. These are real live conversations between real people, not mixtures, but the participants role-play a design team. The rest are natural meetings. Many speakers are non-native English speakers. That helps make the model robust, but keep it in mind when you build your test sets.
- **NOTSOFAR-1:** The licence is CC BY 4.0, but the repo also says the data is "provided for open research." That line doesn't add a formal restriction, but it's ambiguous enough that you should ask Microsoft for written confirmation before shipping. Also, Dev-set-2 is limited to use within the challenge, so leave it out.
- **ICSI:** The meetings are academic research meetings, so they're not quite business meetings, but they are natural and unscripted. Get it from the Edinburgh distribution, which is the CC BY one, not an older copy.
- **DiPCo:** It's social conversation, not business, and it's small. It's still good for training on hard far-field overlap.

Taken together, this gives you roughly 180 h or more of real, multi-party, far-field English, all with commercial-use licences. NOTSOFAR is the one most like your production setting, so I'd use part of it as your main evaluation set.

## Paid options

- **LDC for-profit membership or per-corpus commercial licence:** This covers the NIST Rich Transcription meeting evaluation sets (RT-02 to RT-09, which are multi-site meetings with distant mics and diarization references) and Mixer 6 (2-person interviews, multi-mic far-field). You get standard benchmarks with commercial terms.
- **Data vendors** such as Appen, Defined.ai and Shaip: they sell or custom-record meeting audio with commercial licences and participant consent. This is the way to get real business meetings at scale if the public data isn't enough.

## Leave these out

- **CHiME-5 / CHiME-6:** non-commercial licence. Watch for CHiME-7/8 DASR bundles too: they mix CHiME-6, which is non-commercial, with DiPCo and Mixer 6.
- **AliMeeting, AISHELL-4:** Mandarin.
- **LibriCSS:** replayed and simulated mixtures.
- **Ego4D, MSDWild:** non-commercial or research-only terms.
- **VoxConverse and other YouTube-derived sets:** CC BY covers the labels, but the rights to the underlying audio are unclear.

## Practical notes

1. **Download from the official sources.** Hugging Face mirrors sometimes show the wrong licence. For example, one NOTSOFAR-derived dataset is tagged CC BY-NC.
2. **CC BY and CDLA-Permissive require attribution.** Keep a record of which datasets you used and credit them, for instance in your docs or a NOTICE file.
3. **Have a lawyer look at it quickly.** I'm not a lawyer. The licences above are clear on paper, but someone should check how they apply to your product, for example to trained model weights and to any participant-consent or privacy questions.

Sources:
- [AMI licence](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/corpus/license.shtml)
- [ICSI licence](https://groups.inf.ed.ac.uk/ami/icsi/license.shtml)
- [NOTSOFAR-1 repo](https://github.com/microsoft/NOTSOFAR1-Challenge)
- [NOTSOFAR-1 paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.08887v1)
- [NSF-QA derived dataset (licence tagging example)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/popcornell/NSF-QA)
- [DiPCo on Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/records/8122551)
- [DiPCo paper](https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2020/segbroeck20_interspeech.pdf)
- [Amazon DiPCo announcement](https://www.amazon.science/blog/amazon-releases-new-public-data-set-to-help-address-cocktail-party-problem)

graders.name: 01-recall-galaxy-zoo-2
graders.evidence:
## Recommendation

Use **Galaxy Zoo DECaLS/DESI volunteer votes with bundled images: `mwalmsley/gz_desi` on Hugging Face**. It has about 400k rows (319,530 train and 79,883 test) and loads with one line of Python. Use **`mwalmsley/gz2`** (about 191k rows of SDSS images) as a second dataset or for comparison with published work. Both have the labels you named, the labels are human volunteer votes, and you can download them today with no account.

## What I assumed you need
- **R1 (must):** at least 40,000 labelled galaxies.
- **R2 (must):** detailed labels for bars, spiral arms, bulge size and mergers, not just a few coarse classes.
- **R3 (must):** labels come from people (volunteers or experts), not from model predictions.
- **R4 (nice to have):** images come with the labels.
- **R5 (must):** free, and use in a master's thesis is allowed.

## Shortlist (checked 2026-11-12)
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `mwalmsley/gz_desi` (DECaLS images + GZ DECaLS/DESI votes) | Open download | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 319,530 + 79,883 rows, ~17.5 GB | Strong | today |
| 2 | `mwalmsley/gz2` (SDSS images + GZ2 votes) | Open download | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 172,377 + 18,797, ~2.6 GB | Strong | today |
| 3 | `mwalmsley/gz_evo` (all campaigns combined) | Open download | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 664,219 + 141,760, ~18 GB | Strong | today |
| 4 | `mwalmsley/gz_hubble` | Open download | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 77,158 + 19,291, ~6.4 GB | Strong (distant galaxies) | today |
| 5 | `mwalmsley/gz_ukidss` (near-infrared) | Open download | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 56,676 + 14,169 | Partial | today |
| 6 | `mwalmsley/gz_euclid` | Open download | no licence stated | 169,899 + 2,378 | Partial | today |
| 7 | `mwalmsley/gz_candels` | Open download | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | ~48k total | Partial (just over 40k) | today |
| 8 | Kaggle "Galaxy Zoo – The Galaxy Challenge" | Free Kaggle account, accept the rules | Competition rules | 61,578 training images | Partial | from memory |

## Details
- **How the labels look (checked today in `gz_desi`'s feature list):** each answer has a vote-count column, for example `bar-dr5_strong`, `bar-dr5_weak`, `bulge-size-dr5_small`. Each also has a `_fraction` column, and each question has a `*_total-votes` column. The dataset card describes the data as "galaxy images and volunteer labels" and lists the annotation source as `crowdsourced`. Today the Hugging Face API reports `gated=false` for all seven datasets.
- **Steps (minutes):**

graders.name: 01-recall-galaxy-zoo-2
graders.evidence:
**Download Galaxy Zoo Evo (`mwalmsley/gz_evo` on Hugging Face).** It has about 806k galaxy images with the raw volunteer vote counts for each answer, stored together in the same rows. It meets every requirement you gave. If you want a smaller, single-survey set, start with **GZ2** (`mwalmsley/gz2`, about 209k galaxies) or **GZ DECaLS** (about 314k).

The dataset-registry search tool couldn't connect from this sandbox, and Zenodo refused my page requests. So everything below was checked on 2026-11-12 by web search and by fetching the pages, except where I mark it otherwise.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:** free images; detailed labels (bar, spiral arms, bulge size, merger); labels from humans, not model predictions; at least 40k galaxies.
- **Nice to have:** images and labels in one package; a licence that allows academic use. I assumed you don't need commercial use.

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Galaxy Zoo Evo | free Hugging Face login, minutes | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | 805,979 images, about 18 GB | strong | today |
| 2 | GZ2 (`mwalmsley/gz2`) | free Hugging Face login, minutes | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | about 209k galaxies, about 2.3 GB | strong | today |
| 3 | GZ DECaLS (Walmsley+2022) | open download from Zenodo | not confirmed | 314k galaxies, about 100 GB of PNGs | strong | from the paper; Zenodo blocked |
| 4 | GZ Euclid (`mwalmsley/gz_euclid`) | Hugging Face, minutes | not stated on the card | about 170k galaxies | partial | today |
| 5 | GZ Hubble / GZ CANDELS | `galaxy-datasets` package | see #1 | about 96k / about 48k | partial | today |
| 6 | Kaggle Galaxy Challenge | Kaggle account and accept the competition rules | competition rules | 61,578 galaxies | partial | today |

## Details
**1. [Galaxy Zoo Evo](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mwalmsley/gz_evo)**
- **Contents:** 664k training and 142k test images (424×424 pixels) from GZ2/SDSS, GZ DESI/DECaLS, Hubble, CANDELS and UKIDSS.
- **Labels:** columns follow the pattern `question-campaign_answer`. Each holds the number of volunteers who chose that answer, alongside `_fraction` and `_total-votes` columns.
- **Load it:** `load_dataset('mwalmsley/gz_evo', split='train')`. A `tiny` config is available for quick tests.
- **Things to know:**
  - The questions differ between campaigns, so expect many empty (NaN) columns.
  - The number of votes differs from galaxy to galaxy and question to question. The paper recommends a multinomial loss, or a cut such as at least 30 total votes.
  - Two subsets that aren't published yet (`gz_h2o`, `gz_ukidss`) need an access request.
- **Licence:** the dataset card asks that **models trained on the data be released as source code by publication**. Check that this suits your thesis.
- **Paper:** [Galaxy Zoo Evo, arXiv 2512.23691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.23691).

**2. [GZ2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/mwalmsley/gz2)**
- One survey (SDSS) with about 170 votes per galaxy on average, so it is the cleanest single training set.
- Also available as `galaxy_datasets.gz2(root=..., download=True)` from [galaxy-datasets](https://github.com/mwalmsley/galaxy-datasets).
- The label release is Willett et al. 2013 (from memory).

**3. GZ DECaLS**
- Download from [Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.4196266](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4196266), or use the `gz_decals_5` loader (about 230k galaxies). Paper: [MNRAS 509, 3966](https://academic.oup.com/mnras/article/509/3/3966/6378289).
- The imaging is deeper than SDSS, which helps with faint features such as tidal tails from mergers.
- **Use only the `gz_decals_volunteers_*.csv` files.** `gz_decals_auto_posteriors.csv` contains model predictions.
- About 140k galaxies have 30 or more votes; the rest have about 5 each.

**4. GZ Euclid:** 169,899 training galaxies, but each has only about 5 volunteer votes, so the labels are noisy.

**5. GZ Hubble / GZ CANDELS:** high-redshift galaxies imaged by Hubble. Useful for domain-shift experiments.

**6. [Kaggle Galaxy Challenge](https://www.kaggle.com/c/galaxy-zoo-the-galaxy-challenge/data):** 61,578 GZ2 images with 37 vote-fraction outputs. It is the classic CNN baseline, but #2 is a larger version of the same data. I couldn't read the competition rules page.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Licence of the GZ DECaLS Zenodo record:** Zenodo refused my connections. Check the latest version of the record yourself.
- **Licence of `gz_euclid`:** the dataset card doesn't state one.

## Not recommended, and why
- **GZ DESI catalogue (8.7M) and GZ Euclid Q1 catalogue (378k)** on [data.galaxyzoo.org](https://data.galaxyzoo.org/): these labels are Zoobot predictions, not human votes. The volunteer-labelled part of GZ DESI is already in Galaxy Zoo Evo. The `galaxy-datasets` README wrongly lists the 8.7M as "volunteer votes".
- **[Galaxy10 DECaLS/SDSS](https://astronn.readthedocs.io/en/latest/galaxy10.html):** about 17.7k and 21.8k galaxies with 10 coarse classes. Too small and not detailed enough.
- **GZ1:** about 900k galaxies, but labelled only as elliptical, spiral or merger. No bars or bulge.
- **Nair & Abraham 2010 and EFIGI:** expert labels, but only about 14k and about 4.5k galaxies (from memory).

## What I could not find
I know of no expert-labelled set with 40k or more galaxies. Every human-labelled set at that scale comes from Galaxy Zoo volunteers.

## Next step
Run `load_dataset('mwalmsley/gz_evo', name='tiny')` to look at the columns. Then train on GZ2 alone, or on GZ2 plus the DECaLS campaigns from Evo, with a vote-count loss.

I also built an interactive page that lets you filter and compare these datasets: `/private/tmp/e-od8sHE/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`

- Also available as `galaxy_datasets.gz2(root=..., download=True)` from [galaxy-datasets](https://github.com/mwalmsley/galaxy-datasets).

**3. GZ DECaLS**

**6. [Kaggle Galaxy Challenge](https://www.kaggle.com/c/galaxy-zoo-the-galaxy-challenge/data):** 61,578 GZ2 images with 37 vote-fraction outputs. It is the classic CNN baseline, but #2 is a larger version of the same data. I couldn't read the competition rules page.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Licence of the GZ DECaLS Zenodo record:** Zenodo refused my connections. Check the latest version of the record yourself.
- **Licence of `gz_euclid`:** the dataset card doesn't state one.

## Not recommended, and why
- **GZ DESI catalogue (8.7M) and GZ Euclid Q1 catalogue (378k)** on [data.galaxyzoo.org](https://data.galaxyzoo.org/): these labels are Zoobot predictions, not human votes. The volunteer-labelled part of GZ DESI is already in Galaxy Zoo Evo. The `galaxy-datasets` README wrongly lists the 8.7M as "volunteer votes".

- **Nair & Abraham 2010 and EFIGI:** expert labels, but only about 14k and about 4.5k galaxies (from memory).

Run `load_dataset('mwalmsley/gz_evo', name='tiny')` to look at the columns. Then train on GZ2 alone, or on GZ2 plus the DECaLS campaigns from Evo, with a vote-count loss.

## What I assumed you need
- **Must have:**
  - galaxy images, ideally in the same release as the labels;
  - labels for bars, spiral arms, bulge size and mergers;
  - labels made by people, not a model;
  - at least 40k galaxies;
  - free to download now.
- **Nice to have:** a licence that lets you publish the work (CC BY is fine for a thesis).

## Shortlist
| # | Dataset | Access | Licence | Size | Fit | Checked |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Galaxy Zoo DECaLS | open download | CC BY 4.0 | 314k galaxies (~230k in the latest phase), ~104 GB of PNGs | strong | today |
| 2 | Galaxy Zoo 2 images + Hart et al. 2016 vote table | open download | CC BY 4.0 | 243k images, labels for 240k galaxies, 3.4 GB | strong | today |
| 3 | `galaxy-datasets` Python package | `pip install` | code is GPL-3; data keeps each release's licence | GZ2 ~210k, DECaLS ~230k, Hubble ~106k, CANDELS ~50k | strong | today |
| 4 | Kaggle Galaxy Zoo Challenge | free Kaggle account and accepting the competition rules | rules not read | 61,578 images, 1.9 GB | strong | today |
| 5 | Galaxy Zoo UKIDSS (near-infrared) | open download | CC BY 4.0 | 71k galaxies, 7.9 GB | partial | today |
| 6 | Galaxy Zoo: Cosmic Dawn (high redshift) | open download | CC BY 4.0 | just over 41k galaxies, ~5 GB | partial | today |

## Details
**1. Galaxy Zoo DECaLS** – https://zenodo.org/records/4573248
- **Images:** four PNG zips (~104 GB total) of the images volunteers were shown.
- **Labels:** the volunteer votes are in `gz_decals_volunteers_5.parquet` (and `_1_and_2`).
- **Avoid:** `gz_decals_auto_posteriors`. Those are CNN predictions, which your rule excludes.
- **Why it's the best fit:** the imaging is deeper than SDSS, so weak bars, spiral arms and tidal features show up better. The questions were designed to pick up mergers and weak bars. The question list (strong/weak bar, number and winding of arms, bulge size, merging) is from my memory of the paper; `schema.md` lists the columns.
- **Caveat:** many galaxies got only about 5 votes, and about 140k got 30 or more. Weight or filter by vote count.
- **Paper:** Walmsley et al. 2022, MNRAS, [10.1093/mnras/stab2093](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stab2093).

**2. Galaxy Zoo 2**
- **Images:** https://zenodo.org/records/3565489. It contains `images_gz2.zip` plus `gz2_filename_mapping.csv`, which links each image (`asset_id`) to its SDSS object ID (`objid`).
- **Labels:** https://gz2hart.s3.amazonaws.com/gz2_hart16.csv.gz (this link is listed on data.galaxyzoo.org).
- **Joining:** match the mapping file's `objid` to the vote table, and `asset_id` to the image file name. Drop mapping rows that have no image.
- **Caveats:** SDSS images are shallower, so weak bars and faint tidal features are missed more often. Mergers appear only as one answer under "odd features", not as their own question.

**3. `galaxy-datasets`** – https://github.com/mwalmsley/galaxy-datasets
- **What it does:** `gz2(root=..., download=True)` downloads the images and label tables together, ready for training. It also covers Galaxy Zoo Hubble and CANDELS, whose official releases have labels but no images.
- **Caveats:**
  - Its `gz_desi` and `gz_euclid` datasets are model predictions, so skip them.
  - The README says some datasets can only be downloaded internally, so check the one you want before relying on it.

**4. Kaggle Galaxy Challenge** – https://www.kaggle.com/c/galaxy-zoo-the-galaxy-challenge
- **Contents:** 424×424 GZ2 images in one zip, with 37 columns of volunteer vote fractions.
- **Why use it:** it's the most common benchmark, so it's the easiest way to compare against published CNNs.
- **Caveats:**
  - Only the training set has labels.
  - The vote fractions are weighted down the question tree rather than raw counts.
  - The IDs are random, so you can't match galaxies back to SDSS.
  - I didn't read the rules page, so check the terms for using the data after the competition.
- **Paper:** Dieleman et al. 2015, MNRAS, [10.1093/mnras/stv632](https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stv632).

**5. Galaxy Zoo UKIDSS** – https://zenodo.org/records/13357341
- 70,845 near-infrared JPGs plus volunteer votes, using the same questions as GZ2. Useful for a chapter on how your model handles a different wavelength band.

**6. Galaxy Zoo: Cosmic Dawn** – https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17200992
- Volunteer votes plus images. It also includes separate Zoobot prediction files, which you should skip.
- The questions aren't listed on the record page; the notebook included in the record may describe them.
- It's barely over your 40k minimum, the galaxies are faint, and it's a 2026 release with little prior use.

## Known, not confirmed
- **Galaxy Zoo Hubble (113,705 galaxies) and CANDELS (49,555):** the volunteer vote tables are on data.galaxyzoo.org, but there is no image download there. The only image source I found is `galaxy-datasets`, and I didn't confirm that those downloads are public.

## Not recommended, and why
- **Galaxy Zoo DESI (8.7M galaxies) and the Euclid Q1 catalogue:** their labels are Zoobot model predictions. The human votes behind DESI are the DECaLS ones in #1.
- **Galaxy10 SDSS / DECaLS:** about 22k and 18k galaxies in 10 broad classes (sizes from memory). Too small and too coarse.
- **Nair & Abraham 2010:** 14,034 galaxies labelled by experts. Too small to train on, but a strong expert test set for checking your model's bar calls.
- **EFIGI:** about 4.5k galaxies (from memory). Far too small.
- **Galaxy Zoo 1:** only elliptical, spiral or merger. No bars, arms or bulge.
- **Hugging Face re-uploads of GZ2:** label tables only, no images. Use the official releases.

## What I could not find
No set of 40k or more galaxies labelled by experts exists; the expert sets I found are all under 15k. Zenodo's API kept failing to respond, so I read the file lists from the record pages instead.

## Next step
Get `gz_decals_volunteers_5.parquet` and `schema.md` from the DECaLS record now; they're small. Start the image download, and while it runs, prototype on Galaxy Zoo 2 (3.4 GB). Later, you could use the Nair & Abraham catalogue as an expert-labelled test set.

The interactive shortlist is at `/private/tmp/e-KrIpti/home/cwd/dataset-shortlist.html`.

Sources: [Kaggle data page](https://www.kaggle.com/c/galaxy-zoo-the-galaxy-challenge/data), [data.galaxyzoo.org](https://data.galaxyzoo.org/), [galaxy-datasets](https://github.com/mwalmsley/galaxy-datasets), and the Zenodo records linked above.

graders.name: 01-recall-galaxy-zoo-2
graders.evidence:
I'd go with **Galaxy Zoo 2 (GZ2)**, downloaded through Mike Walmsley's `galaxy-datasets` Python package. It's free, and the images and labels come together in one download. You get about 210k SDSS galaxies, all labelled by volunteer votes, so you're well past 40k.

### Why GZ2 fits
- **The labels cover what you listed.** The GZ2 decision tree asks about bars, whether there are spiral arms, how many arms and how tightly wound, how prominent the bulge is, edge-on discs and bulge shape, and odd features including mergers and tidal debris.
- **The labels are human.** Each question has vote counts and vote fractions from about 40–50 volunteers per galaxy. The underlying catalogue is Willett et al. 2013, with debiased fractions from Hart et al. 2016.
- **It's easy to load:**
  ```python
  pip install galaxy-datasets

  from galaxy_datasets import gz2
  catalog, label_cols = gz2(root='data/gz2', train=True, download=True)
  # catalog: pandas DataFrame with 'file_loc' (image path) + vote columns
  ```
  There's also a ready-made PyTorch `Dataset`: `from galaxy_datasets.pytorch import GZ2`. Using `train=True` or `train=False` still downloads everything; the flag only picks which split you get back.

### Alternatives in the same package
- **`gz_decals_5`**: about 230k galaxies with volunteer votes. The DECaLS images are deeper than SDSS and show faint features like tidal tails better, so it's the better choice if mergers matter a lot to you. The question tree is a bit different from GZ2's (for example, it has strong vs. weak bar answers and better merger questions).
- **`gz_hubble`** (~106k) and **`gz_candels`** (~50k) are volunteer-labelled too, but they're high-redshift HST galaxies. That's only relevant if your thesis is about distant galaxies.

### Things to avoid
- **GZ DESI (8.7M galaxies) and any table with "auto" or "posterior" in its name.** In the GZ DESI release paper (Walmsley et al. 2023), the 8.7M labels are Zoobot CNN predictions, not votes. That's exactly what you want to keep out of your training data. The package README lists `gz_desi` under "volunteer votes", which doesn't match how I understand that release, so if you ever touch it, check which columns are actual votes. The same goes for the DECaLS DR8 data, which includes automated predictions alongside volunteer votes.
- **Kaggle's "Galaxy Zoo – The Galaxy Challenge"** (about 61.5k GZ2 images with vote fractions). graders.name: 01-recall-galaxy-zoo-2
graders.evidence:
Download **Galaxy Zoo DECaLS (GZD-5)** using Mike Walmsley's `galaxy-datasets` Python package. It gives you images and volunteer vote labels together, and it meets all your requirements.

```bash
pip install galaxy-datasets
```
```python
from galaxy_datasets import gz_decals_5

catalog, label_cols = gz_decals_5(root='data/gz_decals_5', train=True, download=True)
# catalog['file_loc'] = path to each image; label_cols = per-answer volunteer vote counts
# train=False gives the official test split (the whole dataset downloads either way)
```

There's also a PyTorch `Dataset` version: `from galaxy_datasets.pytorch import ...`.

**Why this one:**
- **Size:** about 230k galaxies, far more than your 40k minimum.
- **Human labels:** the labels are counts of how many Galaxy Zoo volunteers gave each answer in the decision tree. They are not model outputs.
- **The features you listed:** the decision tree asks about strong, weak or no bar; whether there are spiral arms, how many, and how tightly wound; bulge size; edge-on bulge shape; and merger or tidal features.
- **Image quality:** the images come from DECaLS, which is deeper and sharper than SDSS, so faint arms and tidal features show up better.

**Pitfalls to avoid:**
- **Don't use GZ DESI.** It's listed next to the others, but its 8.7M labels are mostly predictions from Walmsley's Zoobot model, so they break your human-labels rule.
- **Don't take labels from the automated Zoobot catalogs on Zenodo.** The Galaxy Zoo DECaLS release there includes Zoobot prediction tables alongside the volunteer vote tables. If you ever download the catalogs directly instead of through the package, use only the volunteer vote tables.
- **Galaxy10 DECaLS is too small.** It has about 17.7k galaxies and only 10 coarse classes.

**Alternatives that also use human labels:**
- **Galaxy Zoo 2** (`gz2` in the same package): about 210k SDSS galaxies with a similar decision tree. It's the most cited, but the images are shallower. The debiased vote fractions from Hart et al. 2016 are a good fit for this one.
- **The 2014 Kaggle "Galaxy Zoo" challenge:** about 61k GZ2 images with vote fractions. It's simple, but the labels are weighted, cumulative fractions and the set is smaller.
- **Other surveys in the same package:** GZ Hubble (~106k), GZ CANDELS (~50k) and GZ UKIDSS (~71k), if you want a different survey or a high-redshift sample.

**Tips for training:**
- Use vote fractions or counts as your targets, not hard classes. The questions further down the tree, like bar type or number of arms, are only answered by volunteers who first said the galaxy has a disk. So you should mask or weight by how many volunteers answered each question. Otherwise galaxies with only two or three votes on a question will add noise.
- Zoobot's Dirichlet-multinomial loss on vote counts is the standard way to handle this. It's also a natural baseline to compare your CNN against.
- For your thesis, cite the data release paper (Walmsley et al. 2022, MNRAS 509, 3966 for GZ DECaLS) and acknowledge the Legacy Surveys / DECaLS for the images. The citation text for each dataset is at data.galaxyzoo.org.

I checked the package's GitHub README for the current dataset list and API. I couldn't open the Zenodo record (the connection was reset), so I haven't confirmed the image size or the exact download size. Make sure you have tens of GB of free disk space.

Sources:
- [mwalmsley/galaxy-datasets (GitHub)](https://github.com/mwalmsley/galaxy-datasets)
- [Mike Walmsley on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/mwalmsley)

graders.name: 01-recall-galaxy-zoo-2
graders.evidence:
**Download Galaxy Zoo DECaLS (GZD-5) through the `galaxy-datasets` Python package.** It gives you about 230k galaxies with images and labels together, and the labels are volunteer vote counts. Galaxy Zoo 2 is a good second option and comes through the same package.

```bash
pip install galaxy-datasets
```
```python
from galaxy_datasets import gz_decals_5   # or gz2

catalog, label_cols = gz_decals_5(root='data/gz_decals_5', train=True, download=True)
# catalog: pandas DataFrame with a 'file_loc' column (image path) + vote-count columns
```
The same package has a ready-made PyTorch dataset (`galaxy_datasets.pytorch`) and a Lightning DataModule.

## Why these two

| Dataset | Method | Galaxies | Images | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **GZ DECaLS GZD-5** | `gz_decals_5` | ~230k | DECaLS (deeper than SDSS) | My first choice. The question tree covers your list: strong/weak/no bar, number of spiral arms and how tightly they wind, bulge size, and a merger/disturbance question. Deeper images make faint features like tidal tails easier to see. |
| **Galaxy Zoo 2** | `gz2` | ~210k (main sample) | SDSS | The most-cited benchmark, so your results are easy to compare with other work. The tree is similar (bar, arm count and winding, bulge prominence, "odd" features including mergers). |

Both are far above your 40k minimum.

## Watch out for model-generated labels

- **GZ DESI (`gz_desi`, 8.7M galaxies):** those labels are Zoobot model predictions, not human votes (Walmsley et al. 2023), so it fails your requirement. It's also about 500 GB.
- **The raw GZ DECaLS release on Zenodo / data.galaxyzoo.org** includes "automated posterior" files from Zoobot next to the volunteer catalogs. If you download from there instead of through the package, use only the volunteer vote files. I haven't checked which files the `gz_decals_5` loader pulls, so confirm the label columns are vote counts, not posteriors.
- Some other entries in the package (GZ Rings, GZ Euclid) may mix in model labels or use a different label process, so check their papers before using them. GZ Hubble (~106k) and GZ CANDELS (~50k) are volunteer-labelled, but they're high-redshift HST images and much harder for this kind of task.

## Tips for your thesis

- **Train on vote fractions, not hard labels.** Galaxy Zoo is a decision tree: a bar question is only asked if the volunteer first said the galaxy is featured and not edge-on. So many galaxies have few or no votes on detailed questions. Either filter by number of votes, or use a loss that weights by vote count (Zoobot uses a Dirichlet-multinomial loss).
- **Mergers are rare.** Expect heavy class imbalance on that question.
- **Licensing:** the code is GPL-3.0. The data is free for research, but you must cite the Galaxy Zoo data release paper (Walmsley et al. 2022 for DECaLS, Willett et al. 2013 for GZ2) and acknowledge the survey (DECaLS/Legacy Surveys or SDSS). data.galaxyzoo.org has the citation text.
- **Small alternatives:** Galaxy10 DECaLS (~17.7k, 10 classes) is too small for you. The Kaggle "Galaxy Zoo – The Galaxy Challenge" (~61k GZ2 images with 37 vote-fraction targets) is fine for a quick start, but the package version is larger and better documented.

The dataset list and counts come from the `galaxy-datasets` GitHub README as of today. The note that GZ DESI labels are model predictions comes from the GZ DESI paper, not the README.
